course.title: Speaking, Argument and Debate
course.description: Build arguments you can defend, take other people's apart fairly, and say it all out loud: structure, delivery, hard questions, persuasion and formal debate.
course.audience: A capable adult who reads and writes well and wants to argue and speak with more clarity and confidence. Has met logic (validity, fallacies) and rhetoric (claim, grounds, warrant; ethos, pathos, logos, kairos) on paper and now wants to use them live. A phone to record practice is helpful.

paragraphs: Here is an argument as you might hear it in a meeting: "We should stop holding the 8 a.m. meeting. People are tired at that hour, and our own survey found that 14 of 20 staff prefer 10 a.m." On paper you could read it twice, check the survey and notice that nothing backs up the claim about tiredness. Aloud, you hear it once, at the speed of speech, and you have a second or two before you have to agree, ask something or answer it.

Reasoning well at that speed mostly takes knowing what to listen for. A spoken argument has the same parts as a written one, a claim, the reasons offered for it and the evidence under those reasons, and it fails in the same few places, so a listener who can hear the parts can find the weak one and ask a single fair question about it. The same knowledge works the other way round when you are the one speaking, because a case built so that a listener can follow it on one hearing is also a case that is hard to knock over.

Speaking also brings things that writing never has to deal with, such as a clock, your own voice, a room that may be sceptical or hostile, and, in a formal debate, judges who have to decide between two cases. A good deal of this can be measured, since a time limit turns into a number of words and a recording gives you your pace, and a persuasive move can be tested for honesty as well as force, by asking whether it would still work if the listener could see exactly how it was made.
outcomes: You'll be able to reconstruct a speaker's argument and find its weakest link.
You'll be able to spot and answer common fallacies in real time without name-calling.
You'll be able to read percentages, risks and denominators correctly in a claim.
You'll be able to state the strongest version of a view you reject before you rebut it.
You'll be able to answer a question out loud in a clear structure and time it to the minute.
You'll be able to manage pace, fillers and nerves with measurable practice.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Logic and Reasoning and English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric.
introduction.length: 12 lessons, about 12 to 15 minutes each. Each ends with an optional writing task of 5 to 15 minutes.

modules.description: Hearing an argument as claim, reasons and evidence, and finding where it can be attacked fairly.

modules.title: Speaking clearly

concepts.title: Claim
concepts.summary: A claim is the statement the speaker wants you to accept.

concepts.title: Reason
concepts.summary: A reason is a statement offered as a ground for believing the claim.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence is a fact, example, statistic or testimony that supports a reason.

concepts.title: Explanation and argument
concepts.summary: An explanation says why something is so when both sides already accept it; an argument tries to make someone accept a claim that is in doubt.

concepts.title: Argument signposts
concepts.summary: Words such as 'because', 'so' and 'therefore' mark a reason or a conclusion, though many arguments have none.

concepts.title: Attacking grounds
concepts.summary: You can ask whether the facts offered are true, current and complete.

concepts.title: Attacking the warrant
concepts.summary: You can ask whether the facts, even if true, really support the claim; the warrant is the general rule that links them.

concepts.title: Qualifier
concepts.summary: A qualifier such as 'probably' or 'in most cases' sets the strength the speaker claims, and a strong claim with weak support is easy to push on.

concepts.title: Exception
concepts.summary: An exception, or rebuttal in Toulmin's term, is a condition under which the warrant fails.

concepts.title: Closed question
concepts.summary: A short yes-or-no question exposes a weak link by making the speaker commit, and is most useful when you already know the likely answer.

concepts.title: Ad hominem
concepts.summary: An ad hominem attack answers the person instead of the argument.

concepts.title: Straw man
concepts.summary: A straw man attacks a weaker, distorted version of the other side's view.

concepts.title: False dilemma
concepts.summary: A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones when others exist.

concepts.title: Hasty generalisation
concepts.summary: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases.

concepts.title: The fallacy fallacy
concepts.summary: Concluding that a claim is false because someone argued for it badly is itself an error: the claim may be true with other support.

concepts.title: Name and redirect
concepts.summary: A calm reply restates what was done and returns to the argument: 'That's about me, not the plan. Can we look at the cost figure?'

concepts.title: Absolute and relative change
concepts.summary: Absolute change is the difference between two numbers; relative change is that difference as a fraction of the starting number.

concepts.title: Percentage point
concepts.summary: A percentage point is the difference between two percentages, which is not the same as a percent change.

concepts.title: Denominator
concepts.summary: The denominator says what the count is a fraction of, and a number without one cannot be judged.

concepts.title: Sample size and selection
concepts.summary: A claim from few or self-selected cases is weaker than the same claim from many random ones.

concepts.title: Compared with what
concepts.summary: Most misleading statistics leave out the comparison, such as the base rate or the other group.

concepts.title: Steelman
concepts.summary: A steelman is the strongest version of the other side's case, stated so that its supporters would accept it.

concepts.title: Rapoport's rules
concepts.summary: State the other view so fairly that its holder would say 'I wish I'd put it that way'; list your agreements; say what you have learned; only then rebut.

concepts.title: Rebuttal moves
concepts.summary: A rebuttal can deny the evidence, deny the link between evidence and claim, give an exception, or concede and show that your side outweighs it.

concepts.title: Burden of proof
concepts.summary: The burden of proof lies on whoever makes the claim, and it rises with the strength and surprise of the claim.

concepts.title: Concession
concepts.summary: Conceding a point you cannot defend gains credibility and lets you argue from a position of strength.

concepts.title: PREP
concepts.summary: PREP is Point, Reason, Example, Point: answer first, give why, give a case, then restate.

concepts.title: Signposting
concepts.summary: Signposts such as 'first', 'second' and 'so' tell listeners where they are.

concepts.title: Rule of three
concepts.summary: Three points are usually enough to feel complete and few enough to remember.

concepts.title: Speaking time
concepts.summary: At about 150 words a minute, a minute of speech is about 150 words.

concepts.title: Spoken versus written
concepts.summary: Listeners cannot reread, so speech uses shorter sentences, repetition and explicit structure.

concepts.title: Pace
concepts.summary: Pace is words per minute; conversational speech is commonly 120 to 170 words a minute, and slower is often clearer in a large room.

concepts.title: Pause
concepts.summary: A pause marks a point, gives listeners time to take it in, and replaces filler.

concepts.title: Filler rate
concepts.summary: Filler rate is the number of 'um', 'like' and similar words per minute.

concepts.title: Projection and articulation
concepts.summary: Projection is volume carried by breath, and articulation is the clear formation of consonants.

concepts.title: Reappraising nerves
concepts.summary: Describing nervous arousal as excitement rather than trying to calm down improved performance in studies by Alison Wood Brooks (2014).

concepts.title: Key message
concepts.summary: A key message is the one thing you want the listener to remember, in about 20 words or fewer.

concepts.title: Acknowledge, Bridge, Communicate
concepts.summary: ABC answers the question asked, bridges with a short phrase, then says the message.

concepts.title: Hostile framing
concepts.summary: A hostile question may contain a loaded premise; you can restate the question in neutral terms before answering.

concepts.title: Saying you do not know
concepts.summary: Saying 'I don't know, and here is how I'll find out' is honest and sustains credibility.

concepts.title: Direct questions
concepts.summary: A direct yes-or-no question about a fact deserves a direct answer before any bridge.

concepts.title: Audience analysis
concepts.summary: Audience analysis asks what the listeners know, want and fear, and what they will do after hearing you.

concepts.title: Building credibility
concepts.summary: Credibility comes from competence, goodwill and character, and is shown more by preparation, fairness and honesty than by claims about yourself.

concepts.title: Story as evidence
concepts.summary: A story works as evidence when it is representative and tied to the claim, and as decoration when it is not.

concepts.title: Contrast arc
concepts.summary: Many persuasive talks alternate 'what is' with 'what could be', building movement toward a call to action.

concepts.title: Call to action
concepts.summary: A call to action says exactly what the audience should do next, by when.

concepts.title: Framing effect
concepts.summary: The same outcomes described as gains or as losses can lead people to choose differently.

concepts.title: Expected value
concepts.summary: The expected value of a gamble is the sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability.

concepts.title: Influence principles
concepts.summary: Cialdini described reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity (later adding unity) as common levers of compliance.

concepts.title: Persuasion and manipulation
concepts.summary: Persuasion gives the listener true information and reasons they can check; manipulation works by hiding or bypassing them.

concepts.title: Transparency test
concepts.summary: A technique passes if you would be comfortable with the listener seeing exactly how and why you used it.

concepts.title: Four teams
concepts.summary: A British Parliamentary debate has four teams of two: Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government and Closing Opposition.

concepts.title: Speaking order
concepts.summary: The eight speeches go in order: Prime Minister, Leader of the Opposition, Deputy Prime Minister, Deputy Leader of the Opposition, Member for the Government, Member for the Opposition, Government Whip, Opposition Whip.

concepts.title: Time and prep
concepts.summary: Each speech is 7 minutes, and teams receive the motion about 15 minutes before the round.

concepts.title: Point of information
concepts.summary: A point of information is a short interruption offered by the opposing side, allowed after the first minute and before the last minute of a speech.

concepts.title: Ranking
concepts.summary: The four teams are ranked first to fourth for 3, 2, 1 and 0 points; closing teams must add a new extension rather than repeat the opening teams.

concepts.title: Motion analysis
concepts.summary: Motion analysis fixes what the motion asks, who the actors are and what each side must show.

concepts.title: Mechanism and impact
concepts.summary: An argument states a claim, explains the mechanism by which it happens and the impact that matters.

concepts.title: Weighing
concepts.summary: Weighing compares impacts by magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility, and says why yours matter more.

concepts.title: Extension
concepts.summary: An extension is a substantive new argument or analysis from a closing team.

concepts.title: Self-review
concepts.summary: Self-review scores a recorded speech against its role, its matter (content), its manner (delivery) and its use of time.

lessons.title: Hearing an argument

reveal.text: The speech builds up three observations and then says what should follow from them, so the last sentence is where it was heading. The next screen gives the observations and the destination their names.

lead.text: Take the 8 a.m. speech and ask what the speaker wants from you. The answer is the first sentence, "We should stop holding the 8 a.m. meeting", and we call the statement a speaker wants you to accept the **claim**. Everything else in the speech exists to make that one sentence easier to accept, which is why the quickest way to follow a speaker is to say their claim back to yourself in a single sentence.

What are the other sentences doing? The speaker gives two separate grounds, that people are tired at that hour and that staff prefer 10 a.m., and we call each statement offered as a ground for believing the claim a **reason**. A reason is still a statement you might doubt, since you can fairly ask whether people really are tired at 8 a.m., so a reason promises support without yet delivering it. A speaker who offers a claim with reasons behind it is making an **argument**.

What delivers the support is **evidence**: a fact, an example, a statistic or the word of an expert that stands under a reason. In the sorted view of the opening figure the survey, 14 of 20 staff, stands under the second reason, while the first reason has nothing under it. That tells you something useful, because the speaker has simply asserted that people are tired and you are free to ask how they know. Take care with the one thing that often takes evidence's place, which is the speaker's own confidence. A firm voice and a phrase repeated three times *feel* like support, but they are delivery, and they leave the reason exactly as unsupported as before.

reveal.text: The survey stands under the reason about preference and says nothing about tiredness. Whether the 20 were a fair sample of the staff is a different question, and one the speech never answers.

lead.text: A listener gets each sentence once, so good speakers help by marking the structure out loud. They say "my main point is" before the claim, "first" and "second" before the reasons, and they repeat the claim near the end so that it is the last thing you hold. Words like these are called **signposts**, and the small ones, *because* for a ground and *so* or *therefore* for a conclusion, are the ones to listen for.

Signposts are a help, though they are not a test. Many arguments have none at all: "Hours are cut, prices are up and the town is empty. The mall must go" contains neither *because* nor *so*, and you still heard the claim without them. So treat a signpost as a hint about where to look, and let the question "what does this speaker want me to accept?" make the decision.

reveal.text: The claim is the statement that supports nothing further. Words such as *since* and *so* help you find the chain, and the next screen asks when they do and do not mean that someone is arguing.

lead.text: Look at two sentences that both contain *because*. "It's closed because the owner is ill" is said of a pub whose shutters everyone can see, so nobody doubts that it is closed and the speaker is telling us why. Now take "The pub is probably closed, because the lights are off and the door is locked." Here the closure is the open question, and the speaker is trying to bring us to believe it with signs we can check.
We call the first an **explanation**, since it takes the fact for granted and supplies its cause, and the second an argument, since it supports a claim someone might doubt.

afterFigure.text: The test is therefore about the listener and not about the wording: does the audience already accept the thing being supported? This matters in practice because you only need to weigh reasons and evidence when there is something in doubt, and when a speaker dresses up an argument as an explanation, as in "We're cutting the service because it's unpopular", the doubtful part slips by unexamined.

steps.headline: Sort the library speech into claim, reasons and evidence.

workedSteps.text: The speech is: "The library should open on Sundays. Most of its users work on weekdays, and the council's own count shows that last Sunday 90 people tried the door and found it locked." Start with what the speaker wants from you. The first sentence is a recommendation, and the rest is offered as support for it.
workedSteps.math: Claim: the library should open on Sundays

workedSteps.text: Next, list the statements offered as grounds. The speaker gives two, and the second is only implied by the evidence: that people already want to come on Sundays.
Now look under each reason for a fact. The count of 90 stands under reason 2, and nothing stands under reason 1.
workedSteps.math:
Reason 1: most users work on weekdays
Reason 2: people already come on Sundays
Evidence for reason 2: council count, 90 turned away last Sunday
Evidence for reason 1: none

workedSteps.text: Put the pieces into a single standard line you could say back to the speaker.
workedSteps.math: Open on Sundays, because (1) most users work weekdays [no evidence] and (2) people already come on Sundays [90 turned away].

steps.headline: Sort the pool speech into claim, reasons and evidence.

workedSteps.text: The speech is: "The town should keep its swimming pool. It is the only one within 20 miles, and the pool's own records show that 400 children take lessons there every week." The first sentence is the recommendation, so it is the claim.
workedSteps.math: Claim: the town should keep its swimming pool

workedSteps.text: The grounds are the 20-mile gap and the children who rely on the pool for lessons.
workedSteps.math:
Reason 1: it is the only pool within 20 miles
Reason 2: children rely on it for lessons

workedSteps.text: The next step is the evidence under each reason.

reveal.text: Each sentence is a ground, and together they point to a claim nobody said aloud, probably that lunch service has to get faster. Supplying the missing claim is part of hearing the argument.

lessons.orientation: Hear a short speech once and say its claim, its reasons and its evidence, and tell an explanation from an argument.
lessons.nextAction: Use a reconstructed argument to find where it is weakest, by asking what links the reasons to the claim.

blocks.text: Here is a short spoken argument: "We should stop holding the 8 a.m. meeting. People are tired at that hour, and our own survey found that 14 of 20 staff prefer 10 a.m." It is about thirty words, and a listener hears it once, at the speed of speech, with no page to glance back at.

Whether you want to agree with this speaker or challenge them, everything you say next depends on having caught two things in that single hearing: what you are being asked to accept, and what has been offered in support of it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say a speaker's claim in one sentence, sort the rest of what they said into reasons and evidence, and tell an argument from an explanation.
intro.whyItMatters: You can't answer or support an argument until you know exactly what it is, and in a live exchange you get only one hearing.

recap.keyIdea: Hearing an argument means finding the claim first, then the reasons offered for it, then the evidence that stands under each reason.

blocks.text: A claim is the statement the speaker wants you to accept, and it may come first, last or be left unsaid. Reasons are the grounds offered for it, evidence is the fact under a reason, and signposts such as *because* and *so* help you find them without guaranteeing that an argument is present.
When the listener already accepts the thing being supported, you are hearing an explanation, and only when something is in doubt do reasons and evidence need weighing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes a reconstructed argument and asks where it is weakest, starting from the step that links the reasons to the claim.

lessons.title: Finding the weak link

reveal.text: Nobody said the rule aloud, and it is the part worth checking, since plenty of schools with strong results owe them to who enrols rather than to the teaching. The next screen gives it a name.

lead.text: Go back to the gym speaker. The claim is that joining will make you fit, and the facts offered for it, which Stephen Toulmin called the [[grounds|The facts a speaker offers in support of a claim. Met in 'Claim, reason and evidence'.]], are that everyone at the gym is fit. Now ask what has to be true for those facts to support that claim at all.

The link is a general rule, roughly "if a gym's members are fit, it is the gym that made them fit", and we call such a rule the **warrant**, because it is what *warrants* the step from grounds to claim. Speakers rarely say it aloud, since to them it seems too obvious to mention, and that is exactly why it's worth saying for them. Toulmin's own standard example runs the same way: from "Harry was born in Bermuda" we reach "so Harry is a British subject" by way of the warrant that a man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.

Saying the warrant aloud changes what you can do with an argument. You can no longer only agree or disagree with the conclusion, because you now see two separate things that could be wrong: the facts offered, and the rule that carries you from those facts to the claim.

reveal.text: The rule "popular restaurants serve good food" is open to challenge, because places fill up for reasons such as price, position and habit.

lead.text: Look again at Toulmin's Harry sentence, "so *presumably* he is a British subject". A word that says how strongly the speaker is claiming the conclusion is called a **qualifier**. "Certainly" claims the most, "probably" and "in most cases" claim less, and the strength matters because a bold claim on thin support is the easiest kind to push on.

Qualifiers exist because most warrants hold only in general. A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject, but not if both his parents were aliens, and we call a condition under which the warrant fails an **exception**, which Toulmin himself calls a rebuttal. The gym warrant has one as well, namely that the gym might admit only people who are already fit.

Don't conclude from this that every argument is weak because every argument has some exception. A speaker who says "probably" has already allowed for exceptions in general, so the useful question is narrower: does a particular exception apply *here*?

reveal.text: The qualifier sets how strongly the speaker claims, and the exception says where the claim stops. Together they make a claim as strong as its support and no stronger.

lead.text: You now have three places to push on an argument, and each has its own kind of question. You can question the grounds, by asking whether the facts are true, current and complete. You can question the warrant, by asking whether the facts, even if true, really support the claim. Or you can raise an exception, by asking whether a condition that breaks the warrant applies here.

afterFigure.text: Notice the form of each question. A **closed question** can be answered yes or no, and that is its strength: "Does the gym admit only people who are already fit?" makes the speaker commit, and either answer helps you, since a yes concedes the exception and a no gives you a firm statement to hold them to. The best questions are short, neutral and fair, and they name the part of the argument they test.

steps.headline: Find the weak link in the bakery argument.

workedSteps.text: A speaker says: "The bakery on Mill Street always has a long queue, so its bread must be the best in town." First say the claim and the grounds.
workedSteps.math:
Claim: its bread is the best in town
Grounds: the queue is always long

workedSteps.text: Next say the warrant the speaker left unsaid, and notice the qualifier. The word must is a strong one, since it allows no room for exceptions.
workedSteps.math:
Warrant: a long queue means the best bread
Qualifier: must (very strong)

workedSteps.text: Choose where to push, and put it as a closed question.
workedSteps.math: Is it the only bakery on this street?

workedSteps.text: The grounds are easy to check and probably true, but the warrant is shaky because queues form for other reasons too. Check that the question is short, neutral and closed. A yes gives you another reason for the queue, and a no sends you to the next closed question, such as whether it is also the cheapest.

steps.headline: Find the weak link in the speed limit argument.

workedSteps.text: A councillor says: "We cut the limit on Station Road to 20 mph, and accidents there fell from 50 a year to 35, so the cut works." The claim is that the cut works, and the grounds are the fall.
workedSteps.math:
Claim: the cut works
Grounds: accidents fell from 50 to 35

workedSteps.text: The unspoken rule that carries the councillor from the fall to the claim is that a fall after a change was caused by the change. Said aloud, it invites an exception: accidents might already have been falling.
workedSteps.math:
Warrant: a fall after a change was caused by it
Exception: unless accidents were already falling

workedSteps.text: The exception is the place to push, and it needs a closed question.

reveal.text: Douglass states the grounds, which are what the laws do, and leaves the warrant unsaid: a person who is punished for disobedience is being treated as able to choose. Saying it aloud shows why his hearers could not easily reject it.

lessons.orientation: Lay an argument out as grounds, warrant, qualifier and exception, then choose the place to question it and ask a short closed question.

blocks.text: Here is an argument you could hear almost anywhere: "Everyone at our gym is fit, so joining will make you fit." It offers a fact and a conclusion, and for a second it sounds reasonable, yet between the fact and the conclusion there is a step the speaker never says aloud, and the whole argument rests on it.

Telling the speaker they are wrong gives them nothing to answer, and agreeing means accepting a step you haven't examined. What you can do instead is find that unspoken step, notice how strongly the conclusion is being claimed and when it might fail, and then ask one short question that tests the weakest of those places.

recap.keyIdea: An argument can be questioned at its grounds, at its warrant or at an exception, and a short closed question makes the speaker commit.

blocks.text: The grounds are the stated facts, and the warrant is the unspoken general rule that carries them to the claim. A qualifier such as "probably" sets how strong the claim is, and an exception is a condition under which the warrant fails, so the question is whether it applies in this case.
Name the part you are testing and ask a closed question, because "you're wrong" gives the speaker nothing to answer.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at arguments whose flaw is a trick of the whole shape, such as attacking the person or a distorted version of the claim.

lessons.title: Fallacies at speed

reveal.text: The reply says nothing about the plan's figures and a great deal about the man. Fallacies like this can be heard quickly once you know what to listen for.

lead.text: Take the reply from the council meeting: "Of course she wants it; she doesn't even own a car." The speaker asked for a cycle lane, and the reply is about the speaker. When a response answers the person instead of the argument, we call it **ad hominem**, a Latin phrase meaning "to the person". It need not be an insult. A speaker's job, history or motive is fair game when it bears on the point, as with a witness whose honesty is in question, but nothing about owning a car says whether a lane would be used.

A second move leaves the person alone and changes the argument. Suppose she proposes closing one road to cars at school-run times and someone answers, "So you want to stop everyone driving anywhere?" The reply attacks a weaker, distorted version of what she said, and we call it a **straw man**, since a man made of straw is easy to knock down. The test is to set the reply beside what was actually said and see whether the two match.

reveal.text: A asked for an hour, and B answers a different, weaker position that A never took.

lead.text: Two more moves concern the shape of the choices and the size of the evidence. A **false dilemma** offers two options as though they were the only ones: "Either we cut the library's hours or we close it altogether" leaves out trimming something else, borrowing, or cutting a little. A **hasty generalisation** draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases: "Both my neighbours had the flu jab and got ill, so jabs make you ill" rests on two people, who may have caught something just before the jab.

afterFigure.text: What the four share is that each skips a step you would need to take to answer properly. That is also how to hear them at speed, by asking four quick questions of any reply: what is it about, does it match what was said, how many options does it allow, and how many cases does it count?

Shouting "straw man!" fixes very little, because the label alone moves the conversation from the speaker's point to a quarrel about technique, and it gives the audience nothing to compare. A better reply is short, calm and in two parts: say what was just done in plain words, and then return to the argument with a question. "That's about me, not the lane. Can we check the usage figures?" does both.

lead.text: Suppose you catch a real fallacy. What have you shown? Less than it feels like, because you have shown that one argument for the claim fails, and that is all. Someone may say that smoking damages the lungs "because my uncle says so", which is a poor reason for a claim that has a great deal of better support. To conclude that the claim is false because it was argued badly is itself an error, sometimes called the **fallacy fallacy**. The right move is to say that the support offered is weak and ask whether there is any other.

A related care is needed with appeals to authority. Citing a relevant expert is reasonable, since none of us can check everything for ourselves, as when you quote a hospital doctor on the side effects of a drug. The fault lies in citing someone outside their field, or relying on fame alone, and a famous footballer is no authority on arthritis. So ask two things: does this person know this topic, and would other experts on it agree?

steps.headline: Hear, describe and redirect one fallacy at speed.

workedSteps.text: You hear: "Either we ban all cars from the town centre or we accept filthy air." First count the options the speaker allows.
workedSteps.math: Options offered: 2 (ban all cars, or filthy air)

workedSteps.text: Now ask whether those two are the only ones, and others come quickly: a low-emission zone, a charge, better buses.
workedSteps.math: Others: low-emission zone, charge, buses

workedSteps.text: Describe what happened in a sentence the room can check, and say what you want back.
workedSteps.math: "That gives us two choices. Is there something in between, such as a low-emission zone?"

workedSteps.text: Check what you are not claiming. The speaker's aim, cleaner air, may be right, and you have asked for a better argument without rejecting the aim.

steps.headline: Describe a straw man and redirect, from a speed limit proposal.

workedSteps.text: A proposes a 20 mph limit near the school, and B replies: "So you want everyone to crawl everywhere at 20?" Compare A's words with B's version of them.
workedSteps.math:
A: a 20 mph limit near the school
B: everyone to crawl everywhere at 20

workedSteps.text: B's version has stretched the limit from near the school to everywhere, and that is where the two versions part.
The last step is to describe the difference calmly and hand the conversation back.
You have shown that B answered a different proposal. You have not shown that B's view of speed limits is wrong, only that this reply did not meet A's actual proposal.

reveal.text: B has found a genuinely weak reason, but the bypass might still cut journey times. The fair reply asks A what the evidence is, such as measured traffic on similar roads.

lessons.orientation: Recognise ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma and hasty generalisation as they are spoken, and answer calmly without treating a fallacy as proof that a conclusion is false.
lessons.nextAction: Read percentages, relative and absolute change and percentage points in a spoken claim, and ask what it is compared with.

blocks.text: Suppose a speaker at a council meeting proposes a new cycle lane, and someone replies: "Of course she wants it; she doesn't even own a car." The reply takes one sentence and may well get a laugh, and yet the question the meeting is there to settle, whether the lane would be used, hasn't been touched.

Moves like this are called fallacies, and in an essay you could point to the line where the argument changed subject and take your time over it. Spoken aloud, you have a second or two before the room moves on, which is why it helps to know the few shapes these moves usually take.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to recognise four common fallacies as they are spoken, reply to each with one calm sentence, and avoid treating a fallacy as proof that a conclusion is false.
intro.whyItMatters: Naming a fallacy aloud only helps if it gets the discussion back to the argument, and a clumsy label tends to start a quarrel.

recap.keyIdea: A fallacy is a move that skips a step in the argument, so you answer it by saying what was done and returning to the argument, and a fallacy never proves the conclusion false.

blocks.text: An ad hominem answers the person, a straw man answers a distorted version, a false dilemma allows only two options and a hasty generalisation rests on too few cases. A calm reply describes the move in plain words and asks the next question, which keeps the room on the argument.
Catching a fallacy removes one support for a claim, so the claim may still be true on other grounds, and citing a relevant expert is fair where citing fame or an outside field is not.

lessons.title: Numbers in argument

reveal.text: The count of extra women is much smaller than the headline seems to promise. The next screen names the two ways of describing the same change.

lead.text: The headline and your answer describe one change in two ways. The **absolute change** is the plain difference between the two numbers, here 3 − 2 = 1 extra case in each 1,000. The **relative change** is that difference as a fraction of the starting number, here 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5, or 50 percent. Neither is false, but they answer different questions, and the person speaking chooses which to give you.

Relative change makes small numbers sound large, because a start of 2 means that any added case is a big share of it. The mirror case is a treatment that cuts a risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000, which can be sold as "halves your risk" when the absolute change is again one person in a thousand. A speaker who wants a figure to sound dramatic reports the relative change, and one who wants it to sound small reports the absolute change, so the safe habit is to ask for both.

reveal.text: A fall of 3 in 1,000 is 30 percent of the starting 10 in 1,000, yet it still helps only 3 people in each 1,000. The relative figure sounds large because the starting number is small.

lead.text: Write the risks as percentages and a new wrinkle appears. 2 in 1,000 is 0.2 percent and 3 in 1,000 is 0.3 percent, so the risk rose by 0.1 of a percent, but it also rose by 50 percent, and the word *percent* is doing two different jobs. To keep them apart we call the difference between two percentages a **percentage point**, so the pill raises the risk by 0.1 percentage points, and relative to the start by 50 percent.
If you hear that "unemployment rose by 1 percent", you can't tell whether the speaker means 1 point, or a small relative rise such as 4 percent becoming 4.04 percent, so ask which one.

reveal.text: A rise from 5 to 8 percent is 3 percentage points, and it is 60 percent of the starting figure. One change gives two very different numbers, so the first question is which one the speaker means.

lead.text: A vivid number often arrives with no base. Forty accidents happened on Route A last year and 8 on Route B, so Route A sounds five times more dangerous. Route A carries 20,000 cars a day and Route B 1,000, which makes the rate 40 ÷ 20,000 × 1,000 = 2 accidents per 1,000 cars on A, and 8 per 1,000 on B. The **denominator**, the number that says what a count is a fraction of, reversed the verdict, and it is the first thing to ask for when you hear a bare count.

The same habit extends to comparisons. "Half the people who were ill had eaten at the café" sounds damning until you ask how many of the people who were *not* ill also ate there. We can fold all of this into a single question, **compared with what?**, which asks for the starting figure, the other group or the usual rate, and which most misleading statistics leave unanswered.

reveal.text: The new slide hurt 0.5 people per 1,000 users and the old one 0.3. The counts point one way and the rates the other, which is why the first question about a count is how many used it.

lead.text: Two further things can quietly inflate a number. The first is the size and origin of the sample. If a radio phone-in reports that 9 of its 10 callers support a plan, the 10 are few, and they chose to call, which is a very different thing from 10 people picked at random.

The second is the scale of a chart on a slide behind the speaker. Sales were 96 last year and 100 this year, a rise of about 4 percent. Start the axis at zero and the bars are nearly equal, as they should be, and start it at 95 and the second bar looks five times as tall.

afterFigure.text: Both tricks leave every number correct and still mislead, which is why the habit is to ask where the axis starts, how many were asked and how they were chosen, as well as what the figure is compared with.

blocks.text: A headline says that a common pill "raises the risk of a blood clot by 50 percent". Yet the headline gives you only a rise, and a rise tells you nothing until you know what it rose from.

Everything spoken about numbers has the same weakness: the room hears the figure once, at speaking speed, with no table to look back at. So when someone says "50 percent", which questions can you ask out loud before you decide how worried to be?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out absolute and relative change, tell percentage points from percent, and ask the one question that checks a statistic: compared with what?
intro.whyItMatters: Most misleading figures are correct and incomplete, and a quick question aloud exposes what is missing.

recap.keyIdea: A figure means little until you know its starting number, so ask for the absolute and the relative change, the percentage points, the denominator and what it is compared with.

blocks.text: Absolute change is the plain difference, relative change is that difference as a share of the starting figure, and a percentage point is a difference between two percentages. A count needs its denominator before it can be judged, and a sample needs its size and its selection.
When you quote a number yourself, give both the base and the change, so that your listeners are never left to guess which one you mean.

lessons.title: Steelman and rebuttal

reveal.text: The critic answered a position nobody took, which is the move this lesson sets against its opposite.

lead.text: Start with the speech you have to answer: "The firm should move to a four-day week on full pay. In the trial, the team handled the same work in four days, sick days fell, and we have lost three good people this year to firms that offer more flexibility." The tempting reply is the one you just named, the [[straw man|Attacking a weaker, distorted version of what was said. Met in 'Fallacies at speed'.]]. The opposite move has a name too: a **steelman** is the strongest version of the other side's case, stated so that its supporters would accept it as theirs. For this speech it might run that the firm can do the same work in four days, as the trial suggests, and that savings in sick days and recruitment might pay for the extra day off.

Why would you help the other side like this? A fair restatement does three things for you. It shows the room that you understood, so your reply isn't dismissed as a dodge. It makes you answer the best version of the view, so if you win, you have beaten the real thing and not a puppet. And it often shows you that you agree with more than you thought, which narrows the argument to the point that decides it.

reveal.text: The fair version gives the supporters' own reasons, such as the quiet hours and the hiring gain. The others reduce the view to a wish for less work.

lead.text: The philosopher Daniel Dennett, in *Intuition Pumps* (2013), passes on four rules for criticising someone well, which he attributes to the game theorist Anatol Rapoport. First, restate the other person's position so clearly, vividly and fairly that they would say they wish they had put it that way. Second, list any points of agreement, especially those that are not matters of general agreement. Third, mention anything you have learned from them. Only then, fourth, may you say a word of rebuttal or criticism.

afterFigure.text: Notice how different a rebuttal sounds with this ahead of it. "The trial did show the same output, and I hadn't known how far sick days fell, so what I'd want to test is whether a busy month would give the same result" is a reply the proposer is ready to hear.

lead.text: With the fair restatement done, you still have to choose what to attack, and the weak-link work from earlier gives you four moves. You can **deny the evidence**, saying that the trial ran for one week and only volunteers took part. You can **deny the link** between evidence and claim, saying that equal output doesn't show the firm should pay for a day nobody works. You can **give an exception**, noting that the plan can't work for the front desk, which has to be open five days. Or you can **concede and outweigh**, granting that staff would be happier and arguing that the clients' needs matter more.

lead.text: Before you rebut, ask who owes whom what. The **burden of proof** is the duty to give reasons for a claim, and it lies on whoever makes the claim, rising with how strong and how surprising the claim is. "The bus lane will save a few minutes" needs little support, while "the tram will double ridership" needs a great deal. A speaker who adds "prove me wrong" is trying to hand the duty to the listener, and the answer is that the claimant keeps it.

Burden also explains why a concession can help. When the other side has a point you cannot dispute, such as a higher cost, granting it takes the point away from them and shows the room you are fair. You can then argue from a position of strength: "It will cost more, and it saves lives; I'd argue lives outweigh cost." That move, granting a point and then weighing your side against it, is a **concession**.

reveal.text: The claim is a surprising one, so it needs strong support from whoever made it. A challenge to others does not change who owes the reasons.

lessons.orientation: State the strongest fair version of a view you disagree with, choose a rebuttal move, and say who carries the burden of proof.
lessons.nextAction: Turn to speaking itself and answer any question aloud in a clear four-part structure inside a set time.

blocks.text: Here is a proposal: the firm should move to a four-day week on full pay, because in a trial the team handled the same work in four days. The quickest reply is "So you want everyone to stop working on Fridays and let the company fall behind?", and it might well get a laugh.

The trouble with that reply is that the proposal's supporters know it isn't what they said, and so does any listener who hasn't made up their mind, so the laugh costs you the trust of the people you most need to persuade. The alternative is to state the other side's case so fairly that its own supporters would accept it, and only then to say what is wrong with it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to restate a view you reject so its holder would accept it, choose one of four rebuttal moves, and say who carries the burden of proof.
intro.whyItMatters: A fair restatement makes your reply harder to dismiss, and a single well-chosen rebuttal does more than a scattering of objections.

recap.keyIdea: State the other side's case so fairly that its holders would accept it, then rebut the one point that decides the case, and remember that the claimant carries the burden of proof.

blocks.text: A steelman is the strongest fair version of a view, and Rapoport's rules put it first, followed by agreements and what you learned, so that rebuttal comes last. A rebuttal can deny the evidence, deny the link, give an exception, or concede and outweigh.
The burden of proof stays with whoever makes the claim, however the challenge is worded, and a concession you cannot avoid gains you credibility for the points you keep.

lessons.title: The structure of a spoken answer

reveal.text: A listener can't skim ahead the way a reader can, so the answer is most useful at the start. The next screen gives the whole shape.

lead.text: Take the four-day week question and answer it with the answer first. "Yes, I'd pilot it. The reason is that output should hold up while absences fall. For example, our design team tried four days for eight weeks and finished the same number of jobs. So, yes: I'd pilot it for the whole firm." That answer follows a pattern called **PREP**, for Point, Reason, Example, Point, and the figure puts each part in its box.

Why this order? The first point tells the listener what the reasons are for, so each later sentence has somewhere to land. The reason says why, and the example turns the reason into something the listener can picture, which does more to make it stick than another abstract sentence would. The last point closes the loop by repeating the answer, and it is the sentence a listener is most likely to carry out of the room.

steps.headline: Signposts, three points and the ear

lead.text: Even a well-built answer can lose a listener who does not know where it has got to. **Signposting** is saying the structure aloud: "first", "second", "so", "the last reason is".

How many points should an answer hold? A **rule of three** is a good guide, because three points feel complete and are few enough to remember, whereas past three, listeners start to drop the earlier ones.

Finally, a sentence for the ear is not a sentence for the eye. On the page, a long sentence with clauses inside clauses is fine, because the reader can go back over it. A listener can't, so spoken sentences are short, say one thing each, and sometimes repeat a key phrase.

lead.text: A spoken answer has to fit the clock, and the useful thing to know is how much the clock holds. Speakers vary, and about 150 words a minute is a common planning figure, so we will use it for arithmetic. The figure shows a one-minute PREP answer to scale, with the point and the repeated point in 10-second slots, the reason in 15 and the example in 25, and the example takes the largest share because it is the part that makes the reason real.

Planning with seconds and words together stops two common faults. An answer written out in full usually runs far over time, because we write faster than we speak, and an answer with no plan tends to spend its time on the first point. Dividing the time first, and then converting each slot to words, gives you a budget you can check while you practise.

blocks.text: Ask a colleague "Should we move to a four-day week?" and the answer might begin, "Well, it depends, because the company has always done it this way, and there was a trial somewhere, and", arriving at yes forty seconds later. Another colleague says "Yes, I'd pilot it" and then gives the reasons. Both hold the same view, and only one of them can be followed while it is being spoken.

A reader can skim ahead to find the answer, but a listener has only the order in which the speaker chooses to say things, and a clock that keeps running. What shape gives a listener the answer in the first five seconds and still leaves room for the reasons?

lessons.title: Voice, pace and nerves

reveal.text: That figure is called the pace, and it is the first thing a recording lets you measure.

lead.text: The number you just estimated is the talk's **pace**: the count of words divided by the time in minutes, here 450 ÷ 3 = 150. Conversational speech often runs somewhere around 120 to 170 words a minute, and in a large room a somewhat slower pace is often clearer, so the figure shades the target band from 120 to 160 as a working guide and not as a law.
Many speakers rush because they think speed sounds confident. It tends to do the opposite: it flattens emphasis, leaves no time for a point to land, and is one of the ways nerves show.

lead.text: The count you just worked out is the talk's **filler rate**, the number of "um", "like" and similar words per minute. The goal is not to remove every filler, which is impossible and not required, but to replace the habitual ones with silence where silence helps. A **pause** does three jobs: it marks the end of a point, it gives the listener a moment to take the point in, and it fills the gap that a filler was covering. Silence feels much longer to the speaker than to the audience, so a pause that seems enormous to you sounds like confidence.
Set one thing to change at a time, since a speaker who tries to fix pace, fillers and volume together usually fixes none of them.

lead.text: Two more things shape how you sound. **Projection** is volume carried by breath from low in the body and not squeezed from the throat, and **articulation** is the clear formation of consonants. Together they decide whether the back of the room can follow.

Nerves are the other thing. The usual advice is to calm down, but in studies published in 2014 Alison Wood Brooks of Harvard Business School asked people to tell themselves "I am excited" before tasks such as singing and giving a speech, and they tended to do better than people told to calm down. Anxiety and excitement are both high-energy states, so relabelling the feeling is a smaller step than lowering it. Treat this as one tool to try, since it comes from laboratory tasks and will not remove nerves in every speaker.

reveal.text: The two feelings share the same racing heart and quick breath, which is why one is easier to turn into the other than into calm.

blocks.text: Record yourself for a minute and play it back, and most people notice two things they did not expect: they speak faster than they thought, and they say "um" more often than they thought. Neither is a flaw of character, since you can't hear your own speech while you are making it.

The numbers are simple divisions, words by minutes and fillers by minutes, and they turn a vague feeling about how you sound into something you can set a target against. What do those numbers say about you, and what should you change first?

lessons.title: Questions and staying on message

reveal.text: The best answer deals with the worry first and does not repeat the accusation. The next screen gives it a pattern.

lead.text: Before you answer a hard question you need to know what you want the listener to keep. A **key message** is that one thing, in about 20 words or fewer, which is the working limit we use in this course. For the library service it might be: "The library stays open at weekends and nobody loses a job." It is short because you have to be able to say it in one breath, whatever the question was.

A pattern called **ABC** gets you from the question to the message. You **acknowledge** the question and answer what was asked, you use a short **bridge** such as "what matters is", and you **communicate** the key message. This is one common form of the method, used in crisis communication guidance such as the CDC's, and the figure fills it in for two questions. Notice that the bridge comes only after a real answer: a bridge used in place of an answer is simply a dodge with a smile on it.

reveal.text: The message is eleven words, comfortably under 20, and it says something definite that a listener can check and pass on.
The bridge is a phrase and never a paragraph. It comes after a real answer, and the key message follows it.

lead.text: Three situations need a little more care than the pattern gives them. The first is a **direct question**, a yes-or-no question about a fact, such as "Did the system fail on Saturday?" It deserves a direct answer before any bridge, so if it did, the first word is "Yes".

The second is **hostile framing**, a question with a loaded premise folded into it. If you answer "no, it isn't just a way to cut jobs", you have said "cut jobs" in your own voice. You can restate the question in neutral terms first, as "You're asking whether anyone will lose their job", and then answer that.

The third is not knowing. "I don't know the final figure, and I'll confirm it by Friday" is honest and keeps your credibility, whereas "no comment" tends to be heard as concealment, and a guess you later have to take back costs more than the gap would have.

blocks.text: Suppose a reporter asks the head of a library service, "Isn't this just a way to cut jobs?" The question has an accusation folded inside it, which makes it hard to answer well.

A spoken answer is heard once, and most listeners will remember only one thing from it, so the order of what you say matters a great deal: what you answer first, how you move from the question to the point you came to make, and what that point is.

intro.whyItMatters: Hard questions are the part of a talk you cannot fully script, and a pattern keeps you honest and on message at once.

recap.keyIdea: Answer the question that was asked, bridge once, and then say your key message, which should be about 20 words or fewer.

blocks.text: ABC works because the acknowledgement earns the bridge: a real answer comes first, and the message follows it. A direct question about a fact needs a plain yes or no before the bridge, a loaded question is restated in neutral terms, and when you do not know, you say so and say when you will.
Practise by asking yourself six tough questions about your own view, and listen for whether each answer dealt with the question before it moved on.

lead.text: **Audience analysis** asks four things of each room: what they know, what they want, what they fear and what you want them to do afterwards. The manager knows the budget, wants a decision they can defend and fears a bill and a security incident. The staff know their own workload, want less time on first drafts and fear being blamed for errors.

The claim is the same and the talk should not be. The figure shows the order changing, with cost and risk first for the manager and time saved first for the staff, and vocabulary and proof change with it. Aristotle's appeals, which you may have met on paper, are ethos, the speaker's character, pathos, the audience's feelings, and logos, the reasons and evidence, with kairos, the right moment, often added, and you can now use them to decide which one a given room needs more of.

reveal.text: A request for a measurement is a request for evidence, which is the kind of appeal reasons and data belong to.

lead.text: Why should this room believe you? Many speakers open with credentials, and it is the weakest way to answer. Aristotle, in the *Rhetoric*, says that listeners trust a speaker for three things: good sense, good moral character and goodwill. In modern terms these are competence, character and care for the audience's interests, and a list of qualifications speaks only to the first of them.

**Credibility** is better shown than claimed. Preparation shows competence, since a speaker who knows the figures and the objections is plainly competent. Fairness shows goodwill, and the steelman from the earlier lesson is exactly this, because a speaker who states the other side well is plainly not trying to trick the room. Honesty about limits shows character, as when you say that your data covers one region only.

Stories move audiences, so it matters what a story is doing. Suppose a speaker tells of one customer who waited three weeks for a parcel, to support the claim that deliveries are too slow. If most complaints are about late delivery, that customer stands for the pattern, and the story works as **evidence**: a vivid case of a documented problem. If the customer was the one person in a thousand whose parcel was lost in a flood, the story persuades by emotion and the claim gets no support, so it works as decoration.

Two questions test a story. Is the case representative, meaning does it look like most of the cases the claim is about, and is it tied to the claim, meaning does the speaker say exactly what the story shows? A moving story that fails either one is still allowed, since it can warm a room, but it should not be counted as support.

reveal.text: Three in four complaints are about late delivery, so the story is typical of them. Representative and tied to the claim are the two tests for a story used as evidence.

steps.headline: Contrast and the call to action

lead.text: Many persuasive talks have a shape. They describe **what is**, then **what could be**, then what is again, and then what could be again, each time with a little more at stake, so that the audience feels movement in a direction. A talk that stays at what is leaves the audience with a problem and no way out, and one that stays at what could be sounds like a promise.

The line ends in a **call to action**, a statement of exactly what the audience should do next and by when. "Approve the 3-month trial at Monday's meeting" is one, since it names a step and a time. "Think about trying it" is not, because the audience can agree with it and do nothing.

blocks.text: Here is one claim, that staff should use AI tools for first drafts, and two rooms to give it in. In one sits the finance manager who signs off the budget, and in the other sit the people who write the drafts every week. The words of the claim don't change between the rooms, but nearly everything else about a good talk should.

A speech is never given to "people" in general, and the speaker who forgets this either bores the experts or loses the beginners. So what would you change between the two rooms, and what would you keep?

blocks.text: Audience analysis asks what the listeners know, want and fear, and it decides the order, vocabulary and proof. A story is evidence when it is representative of the cases and tied to the claim, and decoration when it is not.

lessons.title: Framing and ethical persuasion

reveal.text: An average over the possible outcomes, weighted by their chances, is the expected value. The next screen puts a name to the calculation.

lead.text: The average you just estimated is an **expected value**. For a gamble with several possible outcomes, we multiply each outcome by its probability and add the results. Programme B can save 600 people with probability one third and 0 with probability two thirds, so its expected number saved is 600 × 1/3 + 0 × 2/3 = 200. If a different programme, Programme A, saves exactly 200 people for certain, then A and B have the same expected value, and what differs is the risk, since B either saves everyone or saves nobody.

reveal.text: Compare your answer with the deaths that a sure programme would produce, which the next screen gives.

lead.text: In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published a study in *Science* that used exactly these programmes. They asked people to imagine a disease expected to kill 600 people and to choose between programmes. Told that Programme A would save 200 people and that Programme B had a one-in-three chance of saving all 600 and a two-in-three chance of saving none, roughly three in four chose A, the sure option. A second group heard the same problem in terms of deaths, where C meant that 400 people would die and D gave a one-in-three chance that nobody would die and a two-in-three chance that all 600 would. Roughly three in four of that group chose D, the gamble. The figure sets the wordings side by side.

afterFigure.text: A and C are the same outcome and B and D are the same gamble, so the answers flipped without any change in the facts. We call this the **framing effect**: the same outcomes described as gains or as losses can lead people to choose differently. Your choice of frame is a choice with consequences for the listener, so honest practice is to give both, "saves 200 of 600, and lets 400 die", and let the listener see that they are the same.

lead.text: Framing is one lever, and the psychologist Robert Cialdini described others in *Influence* (1984). He named six principles of compliance: **reciprocity**, the urge to return a favour; **commitment and consistency**, the wish to act in line with what we have already said; **social proof**, doing what others do; **authority**, deferring to experts; **liking**, saying yes to people we like; and **scarcity**, valuing what is in short supply.

None of these is wrong in itself, and each has an honest use and an abuse. "Most of your neighbours pay on time" is social proof when it is true, and invented reviews are the same principle abused. "Only 3 seats left" is scarcity when the seats really are nearly gone, and manipulation when 40 are free.

lead.text: Where does honest persuasion end? **Persuasion** gives the listener true information and reasons they can check, and **manipulation** works by hiding or bypassing them. Emotion alone does not make the difference: a charity that shows a real person in real need appeals to feeling that fits the facts, and that is honest.

A practical check is the **transparency test**: would you be comfortable with the listener seeing exactly how and why you used the technique? "Most of your neighbours pay on time" can be said openly, because it is true and the listener can check it. "Only 3 left" about an invented shortage works only if the listener doesn't know it is invented, so it would not survive being seen, and that is the sign that it has turned from persuading into manipulating.

reveal.text: The one that fails is the one that depends on the listener not knowing something the speaker knows.

steps.headline: Check a framed claim by saying it in the other frame.

workedSteps.text: A hospital leaflet says: "This surgery has a 90 percent survival rate." Restate it in the frame of losses to see whether the wording is doing the work.
workedSteps.math:
Survive: 90%
Do not survive: 100% − 90% = 10%

workedSteps.text: Put the figure on a number of people, so that the claim is easy to picture.
Decide how to say it. Giving only the survival rate leaves the listener to guess the other half, so give both.
workedSteps.math: "Nine in ten survive, and one in ten do not."

workedSteps.text: Run the transparency test on that sentence. The listener can see exactly what you have done, which is to say one fact two ways, so it passes.

reveal.text: The two descriptions are the same fact. Saying "350 of 500 saved, and 150 lost" lets the audience see that.

blocks.text: A disease is expected to kill 600 people, and a plan to fight it can be described in two ways: "This plan will save 200 people", or "Under this plan 400 people will die." Both sentences are true, and they describe exactly the same outcome.
Listeners don't respond to the two sentences in the same way, which means that the wording you choose is itself a decision that shapes what people do.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out an expected value in a framed problem, name the six influence principles with one honest use and one abuse of each, and apply the transparency test to a technique.
intro.whyItMatters: Every speaker frames, so the choice is whether to do it in the open, and the transparency test gives you a way to decide.

recap.keyIdea: The same facts can be framed as gains or losses, and a technique is honest persuasion when it would survive the listener seeing exactly how and why you used it.

blocks.text: Expected value is each outcome multiplied by its probability and added, and in the disease problem both programmes come to 200 saved, so the wording is what changes the choice. Cialdini's six principles are levers with honest uses and abuses, and scarcity, social proof and authority are honest only when they are true.
Giving both frames, and the true figure behind a social or scarcity claim, is the comfortable way to pass the test.

lessons.title: The British Parliamentary format

reveal.text: Every team is ranked against the other three, so the team that agrees with you is still a rival, and the rest of the lesson shows who the eight speakers are and what rules they follow.

lead.text: The four teams are the Opening Government, the Opening Opposition, the Closing Government and the Closing Opposition, shortened to OG, OO, CG and CO in the figure. The two Government teams argue for the motion and the two Opposition teams argue against it, but there are four rankings to win, so the Closing Government is a rival of the Opening Government even though they are on the same side. The eight speeches alternate between the sides, and the figure numbers them: the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Deputy Leader of the Opposition open the debate, and then the Member for the Government, the Member for the Opposition, the Government Whip and the Opposition Whip close it.

afterFigure.text: The Opening Government defines the motion and makes its case, and the Opening Opposition rebuts that and makes its own. The Closing teams add further arguments of their own, and the two Whips, in the last two speeches, summarise the debate and do not bring in new arguments.

lead.text: The format runs to a clock. Teams are given the motion about 15 minutes before the round to prepare, and each of the eight speeches lasts 7 minutes. During a speech, a speaker on the other side may offer a **point of information**, a short interruption in which they rise and ask for the floor, and the speaker holding the floor may accept or decline. The first and last minute of every speech are **protected time**, when no point may be offered, so the open window runs from the end of the first minute to the start of the last.

Points of information are part of the contest, offered briefly, and the championship manual's guidance is that each speaker should accept at least one and ideally two. A speaker who declines every point can look as though they fear questions.

lead.text: At the end of the round the judges rank all four teams from first to fourth, and the rankings carry 3, 2, 1 and 0 points. Each team is trying to do better than three others, and one of those three is on its own side. That is why a closing team can't simply repeat or summarise what its opening team said. It must offer an **extension**, a new and separate line of argument that gives the judges a reason to rank it above the opening team of its own side.
An extension is judged against what the opening team has already said, so the Member's speech has to be built with the opening team's case in mind.

reveal.text: Repeating the opening team's case gives the judges nothing new, so it cannot earn a higher rank.

blocks.text: British Parliamentary debating is the format of the World Universities Debating Championship, and a round in it has eight speakers in four teams of two. Two teams argue for the motion and two against it, with the speeches alternating between the sides.
Each of the eight speakers has a title and a job, a fixed place in the order and seven minutes on the clock, and the rules about when the other side may interrupt are part of the contest.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the four teams and eight speakers in order, state the times and the protected minutes for points of information, and say what a closing team must add.
intro.whyItMatters: A format's rules decide what a good speech has to do, and knowing them lets you plan your speech for its slot.

recap.keyIdea: A British Parliamentary round has four teams of two, eight 7-minute speeches in a fixed order and a ranking of the teams, with points of information allowed between the protected first and last minutes.

blocks.text: The Opening teams make and rebut the main cases, and the Closing teams must add an extension, because the closing team on your own side is also a rival. The Whips summarise and add no new arguments.
Points of information are offered briefly in the five open minutes of a speech and are part of the format, so a speaker should expect to take at least one.

lessons.title: Building and weighing a case

reveal.text: A large impact with a modest chance has an expected size that can be set beside any other. The lesson comes back to this calculation after the case has been built.

lead.text: Before you build a case you need to know what the round is about. Take the motion "This House would make city buses free." **Motion analysis** asks three things: what the motion is asking, who the actors are, and what each side must show. This motion asks whether free fares would leave cities better off on balance, the actors are councils, riders, drivers and taxpayers, and the figure shows what each side then has to prove. The Government, which proposes the change, must show it would be better, and the Opposition may show that it would not, or that the costs outweigh the gains.

afterFigure.text: Writing the analysis in two sentences before you speak keeps the case tied to the question the judges are actually asking.

lead.text: A list of points is not a case. Compare "Free buses are good" with "Free buses would cut car commuting: with no fare, driving loses its cost advantage, so drivers switch, and fewer cars mean less pollution and fewer asthma attacks." The second states a claim, and it also gives the **mechanism**, the explanation of how the claim would come about, and the **impact**, the thing that matters because it does. The first has neither, which makes it an assertion, and a judge has nothing to weigh in an assertion.

A useful check is to ask "how?" of your claim and "so what?" of your mechanism. If you can answer both in a sentence each, you have an argument. The figure sets the bare assertion beside the full argument.

diagram.alt: Two versions of one point. The bare assertion is a claim that free buses are good with no mechanism and no impact. The argument states the claim, the mechanism by which drivers switch, and the impact of fewer cars and less pollution.

lead.text: Both sides will have impacts, and the judges must decide which weighs more. **Weighing** compares them on named axes: magnitude, how many people are affected and how much; probability, how likely it is; timeframe, how soon; and reversibility, whether it can be undone. One way to put magnitude and probability together is the expected size, the number affected multiplied by the probability. In the figure's first view, Impact A would help 500 people with probability 0.4, an expected 200, and Impact B would help 150 with probability 0.6, an expected 90.

Size is not the end of it, which is why the figure has a second view. A is larger and slower, taking ten years and then being permanent, and B is smaller but arrives next year and could be undone. A bigger impact doesn't always win, and a huge impact with low probability can lose to a modest, near-certain one, so the team must say *why* its axis matters most. A good weighing sentence also concedes what is true: "Even if the other side is right about cost, ours is larger, more likely and cannot be undone." Treating the other side's impacts as zero is rarely believable.

diagram.alt: Two views of weighing. First, bars for the expected size of two impacts: A is 200, from 500 people at probability 0.4, and B is 90, from 150 people at probability 0.6. Second, a table of timeframe and reversibility: A is in ten years and cannot be undone, B is next year and can be undone.
diagram.caption: Size is only one axis. Use the buttons to move from expected size to timeframe and reversibility.

lead.text: For a closing team the case has a further requirement. An **extension**, as the format lesson said, is a substantive new argument or analysis, such as a new group of people affected that the opening bench never mentioned. It has to be built like any other argument, with a mechanism and an impact, and it has to be weighed, since the judges will rank it against the opening team's case as well as the other side's.

How do you improve? Record a 4-minute case and score it. A simple rubric, this course's own and not an official one, has four rows: role, whether the speech did its slot's job; matter, whether the arguments were sound and weighed; manner, whether it was clear and paced; and time, whether it used its minutes as planned. At about 150 words a minute, a full 7-minute speech is a budget of about 1,050 words.
