steps.headline: Build a case for the Government and weigh it against the Opposition's main impact.

workedSteps.text: The motion is "This House would make city buses free", and the Government's claim is that free buses cut car commuting. Give the mechanism and the impact.
workedSteps.math:
Mechanism: with no fare, driving loses its cost edge
Impact: fewer cars, less pollution

workedSteps.text: Put numbers on the impact. Suppose 40,000 commuters could switch, with probability 0.25.
The Opposition's main impact is service cuts that hurt 8,000 riders, with probability 0.5. Work out its expected size on the same scale.
Compare the two, and add the other axes. The Government's is larger by 6,000, and fares could be brought back if cuts began, so the harm is reversible.
Say it as a weighing sentence, conceding what is true.
workedSteps.math: "Even if some services are cut, more people switch and the cuts can be reversed."

steps.headline: Weigh a larger Opposition impact on the same scale.

workedSteps.text: Suppose the Opposition argues instead that the cuts would hurt 12,000 riders, with probability 0.3.
Its expected size goes on the same scale as the Government's 10,000.
The comparison with the Government's 10,000 comes next, along with the other axis, which is that fares can be reintroduced if the cuts begin.

reveal.text: A weighing sentence earns its place by naming axes that a judge can check, and by conceding what is fair.

lessons.orientation: Analyse a motion, build arguments with a mechanism and an impact, and weigh competing impacts by size, probability, timeframe and reversibility.
lessons.nextAction: You can now hear and test an argument, answer questions aloud under a time limit, persuade honestly, and build and weigh a case in a British Parliamentary round.

blocks.text: Suppose one team in a debate claims an impact that would help 1,000 people but has only about a thirty percent chance of happening, while the other team's impact would help 200 people and is almost certain. Each team is right about its own impact, and the judges still have to decide which one matters more.
Rounds like this are usually won by the team that makes the comparison out loud instead of leaving it to the judges.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to analyse a motion, build an argument with a mechanism and an impact, work out the expected size of an impact, and weigh two impacts on size, probability, timeframe and reversibility.
intro.whyItMatters: A case that explains and weighs its impacts gives the judges something to check, and a bare list of claims does not.

recap.keyIdea: Analyse the motion, build each argument with a mechanism and an impact, and weigh your impacts against the other side's on named axes.

blocks.text: A claim with no mechanism is an assertion, and an impact becomes comparable when you put a number on its expected size, the number affected multiplied by the probability. Size is only one axis, so a good weighing also names timeframe and reversibility and concedes what is true on the other side.
A closing team adds an extension, and a recorded 4-minute case scored on role, matter, manner and time shows what to change next.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Hours are cut, prices are up and the town is empty. The mall must go." Which statement is the claim?
hints: Ask which sentence the others are there to support.
Which one tells the listener what to think or do?

acceptedIdeas: The mall must go.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mall must go.

choices.label: Prices are up.
The mall must go.
Hours are cut.
The town is empty.

questions.onCorrect: The first sentence is a list of grounds, and the last is what they are offered for. A claim can come last.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the grounds. Ask which statement the three observations are meant to support.
That is a ground, one of three. The claim is what they add up to.
That is a ground too. The claim is the statement the others are offered for.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Prices will rise next year, since the harvest failed, so we should lock in a contract now." Which statement is the claim?
hints: Look for the word that points forward to what the earlier statements are for.
Some statements rest on an earlier one and support a later one. The claim is the statement that supports nothing further.

acceptedIdeas: We should lock in a contract
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: We should lock in a contract

choices.label: The harvest has failed badly
Prices will rise next year
We should lock in a contract

questions.onCorrect: The word *so* points forward to the conclusion, and *since* points back to a ground. The price rise sits in the middle, resting on the harvest and supporting the advice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a ground, the fact at the bottom of the chain. The claim is what the speaker wants you to accept in the end.
That is a reason. It rests on the harvest and itself supports the advice, and the word *so* points past it to the claim.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "We should stop holding the 8 a.m. meeting. People are tired at that hour, and our own survey found that 14 of 20 staff prefer 10 a.m." What job does the survey sentence do?
hints: Ask which reason the survey could support, and what the survey actually measured.
A reason is a statement you could doubt, and evidence is a fact standing under it. Which statement in the speech does a count of 14 out of 20 stand under?

acceptedIdeas: It is evidence under the reason that staff prefer a later start
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is evidence under the reason that staff prefer a later start

choices.label: It is evidence under the reason that staff prefer a later start
It is the claim, because it is the only sentence with a number in it
It is evidence for the reason that people are tired at that hour

questions.onCorrect: The survey counts how many staff prefer 10 a.m., so it stands under that reason. The reason about tiredness has nothing under it, and you are free to ask how the speaker knows.

misconceptions.feedback: A figure can be evidence, and the claim is the sentence the whole speech is built to make you accept. Here that is the first one, that the meeting should stop.
The survey asked which time staff prefer and says nothing about tiredness, so the first reason still has nothing under it.

questions.prompt: "The bridge will probably flood this spring, because the river rose past the same mark twice in the last three years." Is this an explanation or an argument?
hints: Does the listener already accept that the bridge will flood?
Ask whether the speaker is giving a cause or trying to win agreement.

acceptedIdeas: An argument
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An argument

questions.onCorrect: The flood has not happened, so the speaker is offering grounds for believing it will. The word because does not decide the question.

misconceptions.feedback: An explanation gives the cause of something already accepted. A flood that has not happened is still in doubt, so the speaker is arguing for it.

choices.label: An explanation
An argument

questions.prompt: "Most of its users work on weekdays." Is that a claim, a reason or evidence in the library speech?
hints: It supports the claim, but is anything under it?
Is it the thing the speaker wants accepted, or a ground for it?

acceptedIdeas: A reason
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A reason

questions.onCorrect: It is offered as a ground for opening on Sundays, and no fact is given under it, so it stands as a reason without evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: The claim is what the speaker wants accepted, here opening on Sundays. This statement is offered in its support.
Evidence would be a fact or figure under the statement. Here the statement itself is the ground, with nothing under it.

choices.label: A claim
A reason
Evidence

questions.prompt: Which part of the speech is the evidence under the reason that children rely on the pool?
hints: Evidence is a fact, a count or an example that stands under a reason. Which statement is a count?
The claim is what the speech is for, and the other reason is a ground. Neither of those is a fact standing under the reason about children.

acceptedIdeas: The pool's records of 400 children in lessons each week.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pool's records of 400 children in lessons each week.

choices.label: The town should keep its swimming pool open to everyone.
It is the only pool within twenty miles of the town.
The pool's records of 400 children in lessons each week.

questions.onCorrect: The pool's own records of 400 children taking lessons are a fact standing under the reason that children rely on the pool.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the claim, the statement the whole speech is built to make you accept. Evidence is a fact standing under a reason.
That is a second reason. It is a ground you could doubt, and it has nothing standing under it in this speech.

questions.prompt: A speaker never states a claim but says: "The queue at lunch is twelve minutes long. The café next door serves in four. Half of our regulars haven't been back since March." Which claim are the three sentences pointing to?
hints: Each sentence is a ground. Ask what all three are offered to support.
Think about what the speaker would want done, given these three facts.

acceptedIdeas: Lunch service has to get faster.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lunch service has to get faster.

choices.label: The café next door has better food.
Lunch service has to get faster.
The regulars have stopped eating lunch.
The queue was shorter before March.

questions.onCorrect: When a claim is left unsaid, supplying it yourself, and checking it with the speaker, is part of hearing the argument.

misconceptions.feedback: None of the sentences mentions food. They are about waiting times and customers who stopped coming, and those point to the speed of service.
The third sentence says the regulars haven't come back here, which is offered as a ground, and it supports a claim about the service that drove them away.
The speaker says nothing about the queue before March. The three facts support a recommendation about how fast lunch is served.

questions.prompt: Pericles claims that Athens favours the many instead of the few. Which statement in the passage is evidence for that claim, something a listener could check?
hints: Evidence is a fact or an example standing under a reason, so look for something a listener could compare with what they see.
Two options are a name and a tone of voice. Which one reports something about laws or about how people are chosen for office?

acceptedIdeas: The laws give equal justice, and poverty does not bar public service
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The laws give equal justice, and poverty does not bar public service

choices.label: The city is called a democracy, and the name is the proof
The laws give equal justice, and poverty does not bar public service
Pericles speaks with great confidence about what his city is

extracts.text: Its administration favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy. If we look to the laws, they afford equal justice to all in their private differences; if no social standing, advancement in public life falls to reputation for capacity, class considerations not being allowed to interfere with merit; nor again does poverty bar the way, if a man is able to serve the state, he is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition.
extracts.who: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, the funeral oration of Pericles (translated by Richard Crawley)
extracts.kind: A speech given at a public funeral for Athenian dead, as Thucydides reports it

questions.onCorrect: The laws and the way posts are filled are things an Athenian listener could check against daily life. A name is a label, and confidence is delivery, so neither supports the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage gives the name as a result of the claim, so it cannot also be the proof. A label says nothing about how Athens treats the many.
Confidence is delivery, and it leaves the claim exactly as supported as before. The support in the passage is about the laws and how posts are filled.

questions.prompt: Everyone in the village can see the café is shut, and the owner says: "It's shut because I'm ill." Is that an argument or an explanation?
hints: Does anyone doubt that the café is shut?
Is the speaker trying to win agreement, or give a cause?

acceptedIdeas: An explanation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An explanation

questions.onCorrect: The shutting is already accepted, so the owner is giving its cause rather than supporting a doubtful claim.

misconceptions.feedback: An argument supports a claim in doubt. Everyone can already see the café is shut, so the owner is explaining why.

choices.label: An explanation
An argument for a claim

questions.prompt: Here is an invented speech: "The bus station should open on Sundays. Shift workers have no other way into town, and families need a dry place to wait. Nine of the ten shift workers we asked take the Sunday bus, and a count last Sunday found 300 people waiting outside the closed doors." Sort its five statements into claim, reason and evidence.
hints: Ask of each statement whether it is what the speaker wants you to accept, a ground for it, or a fact standing under a ground.
A survey result or a count is evidence. A statement that still invites the question "how do you know?" is a reason.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The claim is that the station should open on Sundays. The reasons are that shift workers have no other way into town and that families need a dry place to wait. The survey of shift workers and the count of people outside are the evidence under them.

items.label: The bus station should open on Sundays
items.explanation: It is what the whole speech is built to make you accept.

items.label: Shift workers have no other way into town
items.explanation: It is a ground you could doubt, and the survey result stands under it.

items.label: Families need a dry place to wait
items.explanation: It is a second ground, and the count of people outside stands under it.

items.label: Nine of the ten shift workers we asked take the Sunday bus
items.explanation: It is a survey result, a fact that stands under the first reason.

items.label: A count last Sunday found 300 people waiting outside the closed doors
items.explanation: It is a count, a fact that stands under the second reason.

questions.onCorrect: The claim is what the speech is for, each reason is a ground you could doubt, and each piece of evidence is a fact standing under one reason.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Every pupil at Hill School passes their exams, so Hill School must teach well." Which unstated statement does the step from grounds to claim depend on?
hints: The missing statement is a general rule, not a fact about Hill School.
Ask what would have to be true for the grounds to support the claim.

acceptedIdeas: If a school's pupils all pass, its teaching is the reason.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If a school's pupils all pass, its teaching is the reason.

choices.label: Every pupil at Hill School passes their exams.
A school that teaches well has pupils who pass their exams.
If a school's pupils all pass, its teaching is the reason.
Hill School has smaller classes than most schools.

questions.onCorrect: The unsaid rule is the warrant. Without it the grounds say only that the pupils pass, not that the school's teaching is the reason.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs the rule the wrong way round. It starts from good teaching and ends at good results, while the argument starts from the results.
That is the grounds, which the speaker has already said. The missing statement is the rule that carries you from them to the claim.
Small classes might help a school teach well, but the speaker never mentions them. The missing statement links the exam results to the teaching.

questions.prompt: "The restaurant is full every night, so it must serve good food." Which statement is the unspoken rule that carries the speaker from the fact to the claim?
hints: Ask what has to be true for a full restaurant to count as a sign of good food.
The grounds and the claim are both said aloud. The warrant is the one left unsaid.

acceptedIdeas: Full restaurants are full for good food
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Full restaurants are full for good food

choices.label: Full restaurants are full for good food
The restaurant is full every night
The restaurant must serve good food

questions.onCorrect: The rule is open to challenge, because places fill up for reasons such as price, position and habit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grounds, the fact the speaker states aloud. The warrant is the rule that lets that fact support the claim.
That is the claim, what the speaker wants you to accept. The warrant is the unstated rule behind the step to it.

questions.prompt: Is the question "Is it the only bakery on this street?" aimed at the grounds or at the warrant of "The queue is always long, so the bread must be the best"?
hints: The grounds are that the queue is long, which nobody doubts.
The question offers another reason a queue might form.

acceptedIdeas: The warrant, because a queue can form for other reasons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The warrant, because a queue can form for other reasons

questions.onCorrect: The grounds, a long queue, are not in doubt. The warrant, that a long queue means the best bread, is, since a queue can form for other reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: The grounds are that the queue is long, and the question does not dispute that. It asks whether a long queue really shows the best bread.

choices.label: The grounds, because it asks whether the queue is really long
The warrant, because a queue can form for other reasons

questions.prompt: Douglass argues that nobody doubts the slave is a man, because the slaveholders pass laws that punish a slave's disobedience. Which unstated rule does his step from the laws to that claim depend on?
hints: Douglass's grounds are what the laws do. What would have to be true of a person for punishing their disobedience to make sense?
Look for the option about what the law assumes of the person it punishes. The others are about the lawmakers' honesty or the number of crimes.

acceptedIdeas: Nobody is punished for disobedience unless they can answer for it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nobody is punished for disobedience unless they can answer for it

choices.label: Slaveholders are honest men who would not lie about the matter
Nobody is punished for disobedience unless they can answer for it
A crime that has a law against it must be a common crime

extracts.text: Must I undertake to prove that the slave is a man? That point is conceded already. Nobody doubts it. The slaveholders themselves acknowledge it in the enactment of laws for their government. They acknowledge it when they punish disobedience on the part of the slave.
extracts.who: Frederick Douglass, What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
extracts.when: spoken at Rochester, New York, on 5 July 1852
extracts.kind: An oration at Rochester, published the same year as a pamphlet

questions.onCorrect: A law that punishes disobedience treats the person as someone who can choose and answer for the choice. Douglass lets the slaveholders' own statute books supply the warrant, so they cannot easily deny it.

misconceptions.feedback: Douglass does not rely on what they say. He points to what they do, so his step needs no trust in their honesty.
The passage says nothing about how common any crime was. The laws matter because of what it means to punish someone, not because of how often they are used.

questions.prompt: An invented speaker watches a woman arrive at a party and says: "Her coat is soaked and her shoes are caked in mud, so she walked here. People in soaked coats have usually been out in the rain on foot, unless a taxi dropped them far from the door." Which part of the argument is each statement?
hints: The warrant is the general rule that carries you from the facts to the claim.
An exception is a condition under which that rule would fail. Ask which statement, if true, would make the soaked coat a poor sign of walking.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She walked here is the claim. Her soaked coat and muddy shoes are the grounds, the rule about people in soaked coats is the warrant, and a taxi dropping her far from the door is an exception.

items.label: She walked here
items.explanation: It is what the speaker wants you to accept.

items.label: Her coat is soaked
items.explanation: It is a stated fact offered in support of the claim.

items.label: Her shoes are caked in mud
items.explanation: It is a second stated fact offered in support.

items.label: People in soaked coats have usually been out in the rain on foot
items.explanation: It is the general rule that carries the step from the facts to the claim.

items.label: A taxi dropped her far from the door
items.explanation: It is a condition under which the rule fails, so the facts would not support the claim.

questions.onCorrect: The grounds are the stated facts, the warrant is the rule that links them to the claim, and an exception is a condition that would break the rule.

questions.prompt: A small trial gave a new cough syrup to 12 patients, and 9 of them recovered within a week. Which claim fits that support?
hints: Ask how strong the claim should be, given how much support there is.
Nine recoveries in twelve with nothing to compare against leaves room for the cough to clear up anyway.

acceptedIdeas: The syrup may help, and a larger trial should check it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The syrup may help, and a larger trial should check it

choices.label: The syrup cures coughs in three out of four people
The syrup works, because nobody can show that it does not
The syrup may help, and a larger trial should check it

questions.onCorrect: A cautious qualifier such as *may* matches thin support. A bolder claim would need more patients and a group that did not take the syrup.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads a small count as a rate for everyone, and it gives the syrup the credit for recoveries that may have happened anyway.
That hands the burden to the listener. The claimant has to give reasons, and nine recoveries without a comparison group do not show a cure.

questions.prompt: A listener asks the gym speaker: "Did you count the members who left?" Which part of the argument is that question aimed at?
hints: The question asks whether the stated fact is complete.
Which part says that everyone at the gym is fit?

acceptedIdeas: The grounds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The grounds

questions.onCorrect: Counting only the members who stayed could make the gym look better than it is, so the question tests whether the facts are complete.

misconceptions.feedback: The warrant is the general rule behind the step. This question asks whether the stated facts are complete, so it tests the facts.
An exception is a condition under which the warrant fails, such as a gym that admits only people who are already fit. This question asks whether the facts offered are complete.

choices.label: The grounds
The warrant
An exception

questions.prompt: Someone presents a tax plan, and a listener replies: "You can't trust his tax plan; he has been divorced twice." What does the reply actually answer?
hints: Set the reply beside the proposal and ask what it is about.
Does the reply mention anything in the plan?

acceptedIdeas: The man who proposed the plan.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The man who proposed the plan.

choices.label: Whether the plan is affordable.
An exaggerated version of the plan.
The figures in the tax plan.
The man who proposed the plan.

questions.onCorrect: His divorces would matter only if the question were about him, and the question is about the plan.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply mentions no figures at all. It is about the man's divorces, which say nothing about the plan.
Nothing in the reply touches cost. It talks about the man's private life instead.
The reply doesn't restate the plan in any form, exaggerated or not. It leaves the plan aside and talks about the man.

questions.prompt: A says: "We should keep the library open an hour later." B replies: "So you want to waste public money on an empty building?" What is the name of B's move?
hints: Compare what A said with what B says A said.
A is attacked for something A never proposed.

acceptedIdeas: straw man
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: straw man

questions.onCorrect: A asked for one more hour, and B answers a different and weaker position, that the building will stand empty.

misconceptions.feedback: B does not attack A as a person. B attacks a distorted version of A's proposal.
B does not offer two options. B swaps A's proposal for a weaker one.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Everyone in the office hates the new rota." The speaker asked 3 of the 60 staff. What is wrong with the step from what the speaker did to what the speaker claims?
hints: Compare the size of the group the speaker claims about with the size of the group asked.
Two of the options describe fallacies that this speaker has not committed. Which one describes the gap between three and sixty?

acceptedIdeas: Three people out of sixty are too few to speak for everyone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three people out of sixty are too few to speak for everyone

choices.label: Three people out of sixty are too few to speak for everyone
The speaker has described the people who designed the rota
The speaker has offered only two choices, the rota or no rota

questions.onCorrect: Three of sixty is one in twenty, a thin slice that may not be typical. The conclusion about everyone outruns the cases counted.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the claim is about who designed the rota. The fault is in how many people were asked.
The speaker has not set out any choices. The claim covers sixty people on the strength of three answers.

questions.prompt: A councillor proposes keeping the library open an hour later, and someone says: "Of course he wants it; he lives next door." Which reply best returns the discussion to the argument?
hints: A good reply says what was done and then points at the next thing to examine.
Which options keep the later closing time under discussion?

acceptedIdeas: Where I live doesn't show whether people would use the extra hour. Can we check the visitor counts?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Where I live doesn't show whether people would use the extra hour. Can we check the visitor counts?

choices.label: I do live next door, as it happens, and I like the library very much, so I see why it matters to me.
You're wrong, and you know it. You only oppose it because you have never once used the library.
That's a straw man, and it is unfair of you to say it, so I'd ask you to withdraw the remark now.
Where I live doesn't show whether people would use the extra hour. Can we check the visitor counts?

questions.onCorrect: The reply says briefly what the remark was about and hands the room a concrete question about the extra hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That names the wrong move, since nothing the speaker said was distorted, and a label alone gives the room nothing to check.
That is another attack, and it hands the room a quarrel in place of a question about the library.
That answers the personal point and leaves the library alone. The reply should send the discussion back to the proposal.

questions.prompt: "Either we ban all cars from the town centre or we accept filthy air." What is the name of this move?
hints: Count the options the speaker allows.
Are there choices between a total ban and doing nothing?

acceptedIdeas: false dilemma
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: false dilemma

questions.onCorrect: The speaker allows two options only, and a charge or a low-emission zone sits between them.

misconceptions.feedback: A straw man distorts someone's position. Here nobody's view has been restated; two options have been offered as if they were the only ones.

questions.prompt: A says: "The bypass will cut journey times; everybody says so." B replies: "That's a bandwagon argument, so the bypass won't cut journey times." What name is given to B's error?
hints: B has shown that one reason is weak.
Has B shown that the claim itself is false?

acceptedIdeas: fallacy fallacy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fallacy fallacy

questions.onCorrect: Saying that everybody agrees is a weak reason, but the bypass may still cut journey times for other reasons, which B has not examined.

misconceptions.feedback: B does not distort A's claim. B treats a weak reason as proof that the claim is false.
B does not attack A personally. B treats a weak reason as proof that the claim is false.

questions.prompt: "Two of my friends tried the new app and both lost their data, so the app destroys data." What is the name of this move?
hints: Count the cases the conclusion rests on.
How wide is the conclusion compared with two friends?

acceptedIdeas: hasty generalisation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hasty generalisation

questions.onCorrect: A conclusion about the whole app rests on two friends, who may have hit a rare fault that most users never meet.

misconceptions.feedback: A straw man distorts what someone said. Nobody's position is distorted here, because a wide conclusion is drawn from two cases.
A false dilemma limits the options to two. This speaker draws a wide conclusion from two cases.

questions.prompt: Each of these six replies is invented. Which fallacy does each one commit?
hints: For each reply, ask what it is about, whether it matches what was said, how many options it allows and how many cases it counts.
Two replies are about a person, so look first for the ones that never touch the argument.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two replies about how she parks and her exam results are ad hominem. The ban on every car is a straw man, the road or a crash every week is a false dilemma, and the neighbours and the three printers are hasty generalisations.

items.label: Don't listen to her on school funding, because she failed her own exams
items.explanation: It answers the person, and her exam results say nothing about the funding figures.

items.label: Her bike shelter idea is nonsense, because she can't even park straight
items.explanation: It is about how she parks and tells you nothing about the shelter.

items.label: She proposed closing one road at school times, and a councillor replies: "So you want to ban every car in town?"
items.explanation: The reply swaps one road at school times for every car in town.

items.label: Either we widen the road or we accept a crash every week
items.explanation: It allows two options and leaves out others, such as lower speeds or a crossing.

items.label: Two of my neighbours were fined at that camera, so the cameras are only there to raise money
items.explanation: It draws a broad conclusion from two cases.

items.label: All three of our printers jammed this month, so leasing printers is a failed idea
items.explanation: Three machines are too few to judge a whole scheme.

questions.onCorrect: A fallacy skips a step you would need to take to answer properly, and the four quick questions find which step was skipped.

questions.prompt: Someone gives a bad argument for a claim. What can you conclude about the claim?
hints: A fallacy removes one support for the claim.
Ask whether other support might exist.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing yet, because other grounds may exist.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing yet, because other grounds may exist.

choices.label: It is probably false, because its support failed.
It is false, because the argument for it failed.
Nothing yet, because other grounds may exist.
It is true, because nobody has refuted it.

questions.onCorrect: A bad argument removes that support and nothing more, so the claim stands or falls on whatever else can be said for it.

misconceptions.feedback: A fallacy shows that one argument fails. The claim may still be true for other reasons.
A bad argument gives no reason to think the claim true, and a claim is not true just because it has not been refuted. It leaves the question open.
A bad argument for a claim says nothing about how probable the claim is. It leaves the question open.

questions.prompt: Taking a pill raises the risk of a clot from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000, which a headline reports as a 50 percent rise. Roughly how many extra women in each 1,000 does the rise affect?
hints: Compare the two risks per 1,000 directly.
The 50 percent is measured against the starting 2, and not against 1,000.

acceptedIdeas: Just 1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Just 1

choices.label: About 50
About 150
Just 1
About 500

questions.onCorrect: One extra case per 1,000 is the absolute change, and the 50 percent in the headline is the same change as a share of the starting 2.

misconceptions.feedback: The 50 percent is a share of the starting risk of 2 in 1,000, and not a share of all women, so the rise is from 2 cases to 3.
Fifty extra would mean the risk went from 2 to 52 in 1,000, while here it goes from 2 to 3.
Going from 2 to 3 in 1,000 adds one case in each 1,000, far fewer than 150.

questions.prompt: A treatment cuts risk from 10 in 1,000 to 7 in 1,000. By what percent has the risk fallen, relative to the starting figure?
hints: Find the fall in the number of cases first.
Divide the fall by the starting number of cases, 10.
Write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fall is 3, and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3, which is 30% of the starting figure.

questions.onCorrect: A fall of 30 percent sounds large, even though only 3 people in 1,000 are affected by the change.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the absolute fall, 3 cases in 1,000. Divide it by the starting 10 to get the relative fall.
That is the fall in percentage points. The question asks for the relative fall as a percent of the start.

questions.prompt: Unemployment rises from 5 percent to 8 percent, and a minister says it "rose by 3 percent". What should you ask?
hints: The word *percent* is doing two jobs here: a difference between two percentages, and a share of the starting figure.

acceptedIdeas: Whether 3 means percentage points or a relative rise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether 3 means percentage points or a relative rise

choices.label: How many people in the country are unemployed in total
Which month the figures were taken from, and by whom
Whether 3 means percentage points or a relative rise

questions.onCorrect: The rise is 3 percentage points, and it is 60 percent of the starting rate. One change gives two very different numbers, so the first question is which one is meant.

misconceptions.feedback: A total can help, but it does not settle what the minister's 3 percent means. The wording already allows two readings.
The source matters, but the sentence is unclear before you reach it. It could mean two different changes.

questions.prompt: Six people were hurt on the new slide, which 12,000 people used. The old slide hurt 9 people among its 30,000 users. Which statement is fair?
hints: Put each count over the number of people who used that slide.

acceptedIdeas: The new slide hurt more people per thousand users, 0.5 against 0.3
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The new slide hurt more people per thousand users, 0.5 against 0.3

choices.label: The new slide hurt more people per thousand users, 0.5 against 0.3
The old slide is more dangerous, because 9 is more than 6
The two cannot be compared, because they had different users

questions.onCorrect: Half a person per 1,000 users on the new slide, against 0.3 on the old one. The counts point one way and the rates point the other.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger count is not a bigger risk. The old slide had two and a half times as many users, so each count needs its denominator.
Different numbers of users are the reason to compute a rate and not a reason to give up. Injuries per 1,000 users puts both slides on one scale.

questions.prompt: The pill raises the risk of a clot by 1 extra case in every 1,000 women. Which sentence best helps a listener picture the change?
hints: A listener pictures people more easily than percentages.
Scale 1 extra case per 1,000 up to the size of the group named in the sentence.

acceptedIdeas: Among 100,000 women, about 100 more would have a clot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Among 100,000 women, about 100 more would have a clot

choices.label: The pill raises the risk by 50 percent, a rise of one half
The pill raises the risk by 0.1 percent, which is tiny
Among 100,000 women, about 100 more would have a clot

questions.onCorrect: One extra case in 1,000 is 100 extra cases among 100,000 women. A count of people in a group of stated size gives the base and the change together.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the relative change on its own. It hides the starting figure, which is what lets a listener see how big the change is.
0.1 is the rise in percentage points, and *percent* alone leaves two readings. *Tiny* is the speaker's verdict, and a count among a stated number of people lets the listener judge.

questions.prompt: Unemployment rose from 5 percent to 6 percent. Which sentence says so without leaving the room unsure what *percent* means?
hints: Say the plain difference first, then the share of the starting figure.
A percentage point is a difference between two percentages. What is 1 as a share of 5?

acceptedIdeas: It rose by 1 percentage point, which is 20 percent of the old rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rose by 1 percentage point, which is 20 percent of the old rate

choices.label: It rose by 1 percent, since 6 is one more than 5
It rose by 1 percentage point, which is 20 percent of the old rate
It rose by 20 percentage points, a fifth of the starting rate

questions.prompt: A forum poll gets 50 votes from the 400 staff, and 40 of the voters say they read the newsletter, so the speaker claims that 80 percent of staff read it. What percentage of all 400 staff voted at all?

Write the decimal as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Only one staff member in eight voted, and those who choose to vote in a newsletter poll are likely to be the ones who read it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of voters who said yes. The question asks what share of all staff voted.
That is 400 ÷ 50, the wrong way round. Divide the voters by all 400 staff.

questions.prompt: A screening programme lowers a risk from 5 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. By how many percentage points does the risk fall?
hints: Write each risk as a percentage first.
5 in 1,000 is 0.5 percent, and 3 in 1,000 is 0.3 percent.
Subtract the two percentages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 in 1,000 is 0.5% and 3 in 1,000 is 0.3%, so the fall is 0.2 percentage points.

questions.onCorrect: The risk falls by 0.2 percentage points, which is 2 in 1,000 and a relative fall of 40 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the relative fall, a share of the starting risk. The question asks for the fall in percentage points.
That is the fall per 1,000. Write each risk as a percentage, then subtract, to get percentage points.

questions.prompt: Douglass puts two figures side by side. What do they compare?
hints: Ask what is counted in each figure, and who is being compared with whom.
Is the count about what people did, what the law allowed, or what happened afterwards?

acceptedIdeas: How many offences carried death for a black man and for a white man
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How many offences carried death for a black man and for a white man

How many black men and how many white men Virginia put to death
How many crimes black men and white men each committed in Virginia

questions.prompt: A headline says: "Measles cases doubled in our town this year." What do you most need to ask first?

acceptedIdeas: How many cases there were before the doubling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How many cases there were before the doubling

choices.label: Which newspaper printed the story and on what day
How many cases there were before the doubling
Whether measles is more serious than flu

questions.onCorrect: A doubling from 2 cases to 4 is two extra people, and from 200 to 400 it is two hundred. The starting number tells you which this is.

misconceptions.feedback: The source matters later, but a doubled count means little until you know the number it doubled from.

questions.prompt: A speaker proposes a four-day week on full pay. A critic replies: "So you want everyone to stop working on Fridays and let the company fall behind?" What has the critic done to the proposal?

A reply that goes after the evidence would mention the trial or the figures. Does this one?

acceptedIdeas: Answered a weaker version that the speaker never proposed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Answered a weaker version that the speaker never proposed

choices.label: Answered a weaker version that the speaker never proposed
Stated the strongest fair version so that the speaker would accept it
Denied the evidence behind the proposal

questions.prompt: A speaker proposes that staff work from home two days a week. Which restatement of the proposal would its supporters accept as fair?

acceptedIdeas: They think the same work can be done at home, and that quiet days and lower costs help the firm.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They think the same work can be done at home, and that quiet days and lower costs help the firm.

choices.label: They want the office to stand empty two days a week, whatever that does to the firm and its clients.
They think the same work can be done at home, and that quiet days and lower costs help the firm.
They think the office is a waste, because nobody who works there gets any proper work done.
They want to stay at home and do less, because they find the office tiring and the work dull.

questions.onCorrect: A steelman gives the proposal's strongest reasons in terms its supporters would use, so it is the version worth answering.

questions.prompt: "The new bus lane will cut commuting time. A trial last August took 12 minutes off a 40-minute trip." A critic points out that schools were shut and roads were quiet in August. Which rebuttal move is the critic making?
hints: The critic questions the trial itself.

acceptedIdeas: Deny the evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deny the evidence

questions.onCorrect: The critic says the trial's conditions were not typical, which questions the evidence itself and leaves the logic of the claim alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The link is the rule connecting the trial to the claim. The critic does not dispute that rule, only that the trial's conditions were typical.
An exception names a case where the claim cannot hold, such as a front desk that must open five days. This critic questions whether the trial itself was typical.

Deny the link
Give an exception
Concede and outweigh

choices.label: The speaker
The listener

Twenty-eight minutes, seen in one August trial
Three tenths of the journey, seen in one August trial

Give an exception: a hospital pharmacy has to stay open.

Attack the motives: the speaker may want the shops closed.

questions.prompt: Lincoln grants a point to the other side before he says what divided them. Which of the lesson's rebuttal moves does the sentence come closest to?

choices.label: Concede and outweigh: grant that both disliked war, then say what divided them

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Nobody has shown that the new rota will not double sales, so we should adopt it." Where does the burden of proof sit?
hints: Ask who made the claim, and how surprising it is.

acceptedIdeas: On the speaker, who has to show that it will double sales
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On the speaker, who has to show that it will double sales

choices.label: On the speaker, who has to show that it will double sales
On the listeners, who have to show that it will not double sales
On neither side, since neither claim has been proved or refuted

questions.onCorrect: The burden stays with the claimant and rises with how surprising the claim is. A claim nobody has refuted is still a claim without reasons.

questions.prompt: A listener asks: "Should we move to a four-day week?" You think yes. Where in your reply should the yes go?
hints: Listeners cannot skim ahead to find the answer.

acceptedIdeas: First, before the reasons.

choices.label: At the end, after the reasons have built up to it.
First, before the reasons.
In the middle, between two reasons.

questions.onCorrect: A listener who hears the point first knows what the reasons are for, and can follow them with that in mind.

misconceptions.feedback: Building up to the answer suits the speaker, who knows where it is going, while a listener who can't skim ahead hears every reason without knowing what it is for.

questions.prompt: Asked "Should we move to a four-day week?", a speaker builds a PREP answer from four sentences. In what order do they go?

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The point comes first, then the reason, then the example, and the point is repeated at the end.

items: Yes, I'd pilot a four-day week
Output should hold up while absences fall
Our design team tried four days for eight weeks and finished the same jobs
So, yes: I'd pilot it for the whole firm

questions.onCorrect: The answer opens and closes the reply, so each sentence between them has somewhere to land. The example follows the reason because it shows the reason at work.

questions.prompt: Three speakers give the same answer to a question about a new rota. Which one would a listener find easiest to follow?
hints: A listener cannot skim ahead. What would tell them where the answer is going and where it has got to?

acceptedIdeas: I have three reasons. First cost, second morale, third timing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: I have three reasons. First cost, second morale, third timing

choices.label: Cost matters, and then morale does, and timing too, which I will come to
There are a lot of reasons, and costs come into it, and so does morale
I have three reasons. First cost, second morale, third timing

questions.onCorrect: Naming the number of points at the start and marking each one tells the listener where they are, and that is what signposts are for.

misconceptions.feedback: It names three topics but gives no marker for where each one begins and ends, so a listener cannot tell where the answer has got to.

questions.prompt: A 2-minute answer uses a 15-second opening, a 15-second close and three equal points. How many seconds does each point get?

Take away the opening and the close.
Divide what is left by three.
questions.onCorrect: Each point gets 30 seconds, which is long enough for a claim and a reason but not for a long digression.

questions.prompt: A speaker has written a 600-word answer for a 2-minute slot and means to speak at about 150 words a minute. What will happen?

choices.label: It will fit, because 600 words is only 300 words a minute
It will run to about 4 minutes, which is double the 2-minute slot
It will take about 1 minute, because 600 is four times 150

questions.onCorrect: 600 words at 150 a minute is 4 minutes, so the answer runs two minutes over. We write faster than we speak, which is why a full draft nearly always overruns.

misconceptions.feedback: 300 words a minute is twice a comfortable pace and hard to follow. At 150 words a minute a 2-minute slot holds about 300 words.
Four times 150 is 600, and that makes the answer four minutes long and not one. Words divided by the pace gives the minutes.

questions.prompt: At 150 words a minute, which draft of one point fits a 30-second slot?
hints: How many words does the speaker say in one minute, and what part of a minute is 30 seconds?
Half a minute holds half of a minute's words.

acceptedIdeas: A draft of about 75 words

choices.label: A draft of about 75 words
A draft of about 150 words
A draft of about 30 words

misconceptions.feedback: 150 words fill a whole minute, which is twice this slot.
30 is the number of seconds and not the number of words. At 150 words a minute a second holds about 2.5 words, so 30 seconds hold about 75.

questions.prompt: A point has a 50-second slot, again at 150 words a minute. Which draft fits?
hints: Work out how many words a second holds at 150 words a minute.
Multiply that by the 50 seconds in the slot.

acceptedIdeas: A draft of about 125 words
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A draft of about 125 words

choices.label: A draft of about 50 words
A draft of about 125 words
A draft of about 250 words

misconceptions.feedback: 50 is the number of seconds. A second holds about 2.5 words at this pace, so the slot holds more than 50 words.
250 words take 100 seconds, which is two of these slots.

questions.prompt: Your slot is cut from 2 minutes to 90 seconds. Your plan has a 15-second opening, a 15-second close and three 30-second points. Which change keeps the answer sound?
hints: Work out how many seconds remain for the points after the opening and the close.

acceptedIdeas: Keep the three strongest points and shorten each to about 20 seconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep the three strongest points and shorten each to about 20 seconds

choices.label: Speak about a third faster so that every word still fits
Drop the closing point, since the listener will remember it anyway
Keep the three strongest points and shorten each to about 20 seconds

questions.onCorrect: 90 seconds less 30 for the opening and close leaves 60, which is 20 for each of three points. Twenty seconds is about 50 words, enough for a claim and one reason.

misconceptions.feedback: A faster pace flattens emphasis and loses the listener. The plan has to change, and not the speed.

questions.prompt: How many points does Lincoln make in this sentence, and what does the repeated structure do for a listener?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One point said three times, so the ear can hold it as it grows

choices.label: One point said three times, so the ear can hold it as it grows
Three separate points, and the repetition promises three proofs
Three points, which needed first, second and third as signposts

extracts.text: It is altogether fitting and proper that we should do this. But in a larger sense, we cannot dedicate, we cannot consecrate, we cannot hallow this ground.
extracts.when: spoken at the dedication of a cemetery on the battlefield
extracts.kind: A short speech to a crowd gathered at the field, in the middle of the Civil War

questions.onCorrect: The three verbs each say that the speakers cannot make the ground holy, with more weight each time. A spoken sentence can repeat a key phrase because a listener cannot go back over it.

misconceptions.feedback: Each verb restates the same idea. Counting them as three points would ask for three pieces of evidence.

About 50 words a minute
About 1,350 words a minute

The pace is 155 words a minute and the fillers come at 4.5 a minute
The pace is 310 words a minute and the fillers come at 4.5 a minute
