questions.onCorrect: It has eight words, well under the limit, and it says two definite things that a listener can check and pass on.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs to 26 words, which is over the limit, and a listener could not repeat it in one breath.
It is short enough, but it says nothing definite that a listener could check or pass on.

questions.prompt: The system failed on Saturday, and you have answered "Yes, it did." Which key message should follow the bridge?
hints: The message is the one thing listeners should keep.
Which option tells them where things stand now?

acceptedIdeas: "Saturday service is restored and no data was lost."
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: "Saturday service is restored and no data was lost."

choices.label: "The system did not really fail on Saturday."
"We apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused."
"Saturday service is restored and no data was lost."

questions.onCorrect: At nine words it fits well inside the limit, and it tells listeners the two things they most want to know.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes back the yes you have just given, and a listener will hear the contradiction before anything else.
An apology can belong in the acknowledgement, but it tells the listener nothing about where things stand now, which is the message's job.

questions.prompt: A listener asks: "How much will the trial cost?" The speaker replies: "The trial is very popular with staff." What has the speaker done?
hints: Compare what was asked with what was answered.
ABC puts a real answer before the bridge. Did the cost question get one?

acceptedIdeas: Answered a different question from the one asked
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Answered a different question from the one asked

choices.label: Used a bridge to reach the key message at once
Restated the question in neutral terms first
Answered a different question from the one asked

questions.onCorrect: The question was about cost and the reply is about popularity. A listener who asked about cost will hear that as avoiding it, however true the reply is.

misconceptions.feedback: A bridge follows a real answer. Here the cost question got no answer before the message.
The reply never mentions cost and does not restate anything. It moves to another subject.

questions.prompt: Asked "Will the library close?", a speaker says: "What matters is that the weekend service stays open." Which step of ABC is missing before the bridge?
hints: ABC has three steps, and the speaker has shown two of them.
The bridge needs something in front of it. What should the speaker have done with the question?

acceptedIdeas: acknowledge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acknowledge the question and answer it, before the bridge

questions.onCorrect: The speaker bridged and gave a message without acknowledging the question. The question needs a real answer first, or the bridge sounds like a dodge.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply already has a bridge and a message. What is missing comes before the bridge.

questions.prompt: A question contains a loaded premise. Before you answer, what should you do with it?
hints: Repeating the loaded words carries the premise into your voice.
The other option is to put the question in your own neutral words.

acceptedIdeas: Restate it in neutral terms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Restate it in neutral terms

questions.onCorrect: Restating the question in neutral terms lets you answer what is fair in it without adopting its accusation.

misconceptions.feedback: Repeating the loaded wording carries the premise into your own voice. The alternative is to put the question in neutral terms.
That skips the question, and a listener hears evasion. The loaded wording should be put in neutral terms and answered first.

choices.label: Repeat it in the questioner's words
Restate it in neutral terms
Go straight to your key message

questions.prompt: Which opening is best for a sceptical technical audience?
hints: A sceptical technical audience wants to check your claim.
Which opening gives them something to check?

acceptedIdeas: A specific measurement and how it was taken
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A specific measurement and how it was taken

choices.label: A moving story about one customer, with no figures
A list of your qualifications and years of experience
A joke about the topic to put the room at ease
A specific measurement and how it was taken

questions.onCorrect: A measurement and its method give this audience something to test, which is what they came to do.

misconceptions.feedback: A story with no data gives a sceptical technical audience nothing to check.
A joke may warm the room, but it does not meet the need of listeners who want to test the claim.
Credentials ask the audience to trust you. This audience would sooner see the evidence.

questions.prompt: A sceptical engineer says, "Show me the measurement." Which of Aristotle's three appeals does the engineer need most?
hints: The engineer wants reasons and evidence.
Ethos is about character and pathos about feeling.

acceptedIdeas: Logos
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Logos

questions.onCorrect: Logos is the appeal to reason and evidence, and for a listener who asks for a measurement it carries most of the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos rests on the speaker's character. The engineer is asking for evidence, which is another appeal.
Pathos works on feeling. The engineer is asking for evidence, which is another appeal.

choices.label: Ethos
Pathos
Logos

questions.prompt: Of 400 complaints, 300 are about late delivery. A speaker tells the story of one late delivery to support the claim that deliveries are too slow. How is the story working?
hints: Ask whether the case looks like most of the cases the claim is about.
Does the speaker say exactly what the story shows?

acceptedIdeas: As evidence, because it stands for the pattern in most complaints
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As evidence, because it stands for the pattern in most complaints

choices.label: As evidence, because it stands for the pattern in most complaints
As decoration, because one story can never be evidence
As evidence, because it is moving and a listener will remember it

questions.onCorrect: Three in four complaints are about late delivery, so the story is a vivid case of a documented problem. It works as evidence as long as the speaker says what it shows.

misconceptions.feedback: A story can be evidence when it is typical of the cases and tied to the claim. Here three in four complaints are about late delivery.
Being moving makes a story memorable. It counts as evidence only if the case is typical and the speaker ties it to the claim.

questions.prompt: A speaker ends a pitch with: "So let us all think about how we might work better together." What does the close lack?
hints: A call to action says exactly what the audience should do next.
Could a listener agree with this sentence and then do nothing at all?

acceptedIdeas: A step for the audience to take and a time to take it by
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A step for the audience to take and a time to take it by

choices.label: A story that makes the audience feel something
More evidence that the audience will agree with the speaker
A step for the audience to take and a time to take it by

questions.onCorrect: "Think about" can be agreed with and then forgotten. A call to action names a step and a time, as in "approve the trial at Monday's meeting".

misconceptions.feedback: A story warms a room, but the close is the ask. It has to say what to do and by when.
Evidence belongs in the body of the talk. A close that adds more evidence still leaves the audience free to agree and do nothing.

questions.prompt: A 2-minute pitch gives 30 seconds to what is, 30 to what could be, 30 to a story and 15 to the call to action. The speaker wants a 20-second opening. What follows?
hints: Add the four parts, then take that total from the 120 seconds the pitch has.
Compare the time left with the 20 seconds the speaker wants.

acceptedIdeas: It does not fit, so five seconds must come out of another part
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It does not fit, so five seconds must come out of another part

choices.label: It fits, because the plan leaves room for an opening of 20 seconds
It does not fit, so five seconds must come out of another part
The opening can run 20 seconds if the call to action is dropped

questions.onCorrect: The four parts take 105 of the 120 seconds, so 15 are left. A 20-second opening needs 5 seconds from another part.

misconceptions.feedback: The four parts add to 105 seconds, which leaves 15 for the opening, so 20 does not fit.
The ask is what the pitch is for. The 5 seconds should come from another part.

questions.prompt: A 3-minute pitch gives 40 seconds to what is, 40 to what could be, 50 to the evidence and 20 to the call to action. A friend suggests a 45-second opening. What do you tell her?
hints: Add the four parts and take the total from the 180 seconds the pitch has.
Compare what is left with the 45 seconds suggested.

acceptedIdeas: It runs 15 seconds over, because only 30 seconds remain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It runs 15 seconds over, because only 30 seconds remain

choices.label: It runs 15 seconds over, because only 30 seconds remain
It fits, because the parts already add to 150 seconds
It fits if the evidence is cut, since evidence matters least

questions.onCorrect: The parts take 150 of the 180 seconds, so 30 remain, and a 45-second opening is 15 seconds over.

misconceptions.feedback: 150 is what the four parts take. A 3-minute pitch has 180 seconds, so the opening gets the 30 that remain.
Evidence is what makes a claim more than an assertion. A 45-second opening would take its 15 seconds from somewhere else.

questions.prompt: Aristotle writes about persuasion by the speaker's character. A speaker opens a talk by listing her degrees and prizes. Going by the passage, what is the weakness of that opening?
hints: Look at the last sentence of the passage. Where does Aristotle say the persuasion should come from?
A list of degrees is what people think of a speaker before she begins.

acceptedIdeas: Her character has to come through in what she says during the talk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her character has to come through in what she says during the talk

choices.label: Nothing, because we believe good and qualified people more readily
Her character has to come through in what she says during the talk
Qualifications persuade only where exact certainty is possible

extracts.text: We believe good men more fully and more readily than others: this is true generally whatever the question is, and absolutely true where exact certainty is impossible and opinions are divided. This kind of persuasion, like the others, should be achieved by what the speaker says, not by what people think of his character before he begins to speak.
extracts.who: Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book I (translated by W. Rhys Roberts)
extracts.kind: A handbook on the art of persuasion

questions.onCorrect: Aristotle says character should persuade through what the speaker says, and not through what people think of her before she begins. A list of qualifications is the second kind, while preparation, fairness and honesty about limits are the first.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage says we believe good people more readily, and it adds that this has to come from what the speaker says and not from what people think of her beforehand.
The passage says the opposite: we believe good people most where exact certainty is impossible and opinions are divided.

questions.prompt: An invented fundraiser speaks for a hospital ward. Which of Aristotle's three appeals does each statement rely on?
hints: Ethos rests on the speaker's character, pathos on the audience's feelings, and logos on reasons and evidence.
Ask what each statement invites the listener to do: trust the speaker, feel the case or check the reasons.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The twenty years and the speaker's own giving are ethos, the child in the corridor and the listener's mother are pathos, and the admissions and the bed nights are logos.

items.label: I have worked on this ward for twenty years, and I will tell you where it falls short
items.explanation: It rests on the speaker's experience and her honesty about limits.

items.label: I would not ask you for money if I did not give my own
items.explanation: It rests on the speaker's character and goodwill.

items.label: Last winter a child waited all night in a corridor because we had no free bed
items.explanation: It moves the audience through a vivid case.

items.label: Imagine your mother in that corridor, cold and frightened
items.explanation: It asks the audience to feel the situation.

items.label: The ward had 31 more admissions this winter than last, and the same number of beds
items.explanation: It offers figures the audience can check.

items.label: Every pound raised buys a bed night, so 2,000 pounds clears a month of waiting
items.explanation: It offers a reason that links the money to the result.

questions.onCorrect: An appeal is named by what it asks of the listener: trust in the speaker, feeling for the case, or a check on the reasons.

questions.prompt: A speaker tells one unusual case and offers it as proof of a general claim. Is the story working as evidence or as decoration?
hints: Does the story stand for the usual cases?
An unusual case does not represent the others.

acceptedIdeas: Decoration
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decoration

questions.onCorrect: A story is evidence only if it is representative and tied to the claim. An unusual case moves the audience without supporting the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: A story is evidence only if it stands for the usual cases. An unusual case does not.

choices.label: Evidence
Decoration

questions.prompt: Programme B has a one-in-three chance of saving all 600 people and a two-in-three chance of saving none. If the same gamble were run many times, about how many people would it save on average?
hints: Picture the gamble run three times.
About one run in three saves everyone and the other two save nobody.

acceptedIdeas: About 200
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 200

choices.label: About 600
About 300
About 200
None

questions.onCorrect: Over many runs, all 600 are saved about one time in three, which averages out at about 200 a run.

misconceptions.feedback: 600 is what B saves when the one-in-three chance comes off, and two times in three it saves nobody, so the average is well below 600.
300 would be the average if saving everyone and saving nobody were equally likely, but saving nobody is twice as likely.
B saves nobody two times in three, but the third time it saves all 600, so over many runs the average is above zero.

questions.prompt: Programme D has a one-in-three chance that nobody dies and a two-in-three chance that all 600 die. What is the expected number of deaths?
hints: Multiply each outcome by its probability.
Two thirds of 600, plus one third of 0.
Work out what two thirds of 600 comes to; the other branch adds nothing.
questions.onCorrect: Four hundred deaths is exactly what Programme C offers for certain, so C and D are the same in expectation.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected number saved. The question asks for deaths, which weights 600 by two thirds.
That is the worst outcome. Multiply it by its probability of two thirds.

questions.prompt: Two leaflets describe the same operation. One says "Nine in ten patients survive" and the other says "One in ten patients die". Patients like the first one better. What does that show?
hints: Compare the two sentences. Do they report different facts?
If the facts are the same and the reactions differ, what has changed?

acceptedIdeas: That describing one outcome as a gain or a loss changes the response
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That describing one outcome as a gain or a loss changes the response

choices.label: That survival rates are a more accurate measure than death rates
That the first leaflet rests on better evidence than the second
That describing one outcome as a gain or a loss changes the response

questions.onCorrect: Nine in ten surviving and one in ten dying describe one outcome in two frames. Tversky and Kahneman's disease problem showed the same effect, and honest practice gives both frames.

misconceptions.feedback: Both sentences report the same fact, so neither is more accurate. The preference comes from the wording.
Both leaflets rest on the same figure. The evidence has not changed, only the frame.

questions.prompt: A hospital leaflet says that a surgery has a 90 percent survival rate. Which sentence gives both frames for 200 patients?
hints: Turn the percentage into a number of the 200 patients.
The two groups must add up to the 200.

acceptedIdeas: 180 of 200 patients survive and 20 do not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 180 of 200 patients survive and 20 do not

choices.label: 180 of 200 patients survive and 20 do not
90 of 200 patients survive and 110 do not
180 of 200 patients survive and 10 do not

questions.onCorrect: 90 percent of 200 is 180, which leaves 20. Giving both lets the listener see that survival and death are one fact.

misconceptions.feedback: 90 is the percentage and not the number of patients. 90 percent of 200 is 180.
10 is the percentage who do not survive. 10 percent of 200 is 20, and 180 and 20 make the 200.

questions.prompt: One programme has a one-in-five chance of saving 90 people and a four-in-five chance of saving none. Another saves 20 people for certain. A speaker says the first is "clearly better, because it could save 90". What is fair?
hints: Multiply each outcome by its chance and add the results.
Set the sure 20 beside the average of the gamble.

acceptedIdeas: On average the first saves 18 and the second 20, so the second is slightly ahead
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On average the first saves 18 and the second 20, so the second is slightly ahead

choices.label: The speaker is right, because 90 is more than 20
The two are equal, because a one-in-five chance is as good as a sure thing
On average the first saves 18 and the second 20, so the second is slightly ahead

questions.onCorrect: The gamble's expected value is 90 × 1/5 = 18, against 20 for the sure plan. Its best outcome is larger, but it comes one time in five.

misconceptions.feedback: That judges by the best outcome and ignores its chance. The first programme saves 90 only one time in five.
They are not equal: 90 × 1/5 = 18, against 20 for certain. Chance counts for something but it is not the same as certainty.

questions.prompt: A plan is described as one that "lets 150 of 500 people die". Which restatement lets the audience see the whole picture?
hints: Work out how many of the 500 are saved.
Which restatement keeps both numbers in view?

acceptedIdeas: It saves 350 of 500 people and lets 150 die
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It saves 350 of 500 people and lets 150 die

choices.label: It saves 350 of 500 people and lets 150 die
It saves 350 people, which is most of them
It saves 150 of the 500 people

questions.onCorrect: 350 are saved and 150 are lost, and saying both lets the audience see that the two descriptions are the same fact.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses only the gain frame, and "most of them" hides the 150 who are lost. The honest move gives both.
150 is the number who die. The number saved is 350.

questions.prompt: Plan X saves 100 people for certain. Plan Y has a one-in-two chance of saving 200 and a one-in-two chance of saving no one. A speaker says "Y is better, because it could save 200". What is fair?
hints: Multiply each outcome of Y by its chance and add them up.
Set that average beside the 100 that X saves.

acceptedIdeas: They have the same expected value, and Y can save no one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They have the same expected value, and Y can save no one

choices.label: Y is better, because its best outcome is the larger one
X is better, because a sure result always beats a gamble
They have the same expected value, and Y can save no one

questions.onCorrect: Y's expected value is 200 × 1/2 = 100, the same as X. What differs is the risk, since Y either saves 200 or saves no one.

misconceptions.feedback: That judges by the best outcome and ignores its chance. Y saves 200 only half the time.
A sure result does not always win. When expected values are equal, the choice turns on how the listener weighs risk.

questions.prompt: Each of these six lines is invented. Which of Cialdini's principles is at work in each?
hints: Reciprocity is returning a favour, social proof is doing what others do, scarcity is valuing what is in short supply, and authority is deferring to experts.
Ask what each line wants the listener to do: return a favour, follow a crowd, hurry, or trust an expert.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The free coffee is reciprocity, the 8,000 customers and the neighbours are social proof, the three seats and the midnight deadline are scarcity, and the cardiologist is authority.

items.label: A shop gives you a free coffee and then asks you to sign up for its card
items.explanation: A favour creates the urge to return one.

items.label: Over 8,000 customers have rated this course 4.6 out of 5
items.explanation: It points to what many other people have done.

items.label: Most of your neighbours already pay on time
items.explanation: It tells the listener what others do.

items.label: Only three seats are left at this price
items.explanation: It makes something valuable by its short supply.

items.label: The offer ends at midnight tonight
items.explanation: It raises the value of the offer by limiting the time.

items.label: A cardiologist explains the side effects of the drug
items.explanation: It defers to an expert on the topic.

questions.onCorrect: Each principle has an honest use and an abuse, and what separates them is whether the claim is true and the listener could check it.

questions.prompt: Which test best separates persuasion from manipulation?
hints: A technique can work and still be manipulation.
Which test asks about openness to the listener?

acceptedIdeas: Whether you could show the listener exactly how you did it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether you could show the listener exactly how you did it

choices.label: Whether you could show the listener exactly how you did it
Whether the appeal contains any emotion at all, even a little
Whether the technique works on most of the people who hear it
Whether the listener ends up agreeing with the speaker afterwards

questions.onCorrect: A technique that depends on the listener not seeing it is working around their judgement, and the test asks whether it would survive being seen.

misconceptions.feedback: Manipulation often works, so success does not separate the two.
Emotion that fits the facts is part of honest persuasion, so it does not separate the two.
A listener may agree because they were manipulated, so agreement does not separate the two.

questions.prompt: In a British Parliamentary round, two teams argue for the motion and two against it, and the judges rank all four teams from first to fourth. Which teams is the Opening Government competing against?
hints: The judges rank teams, not sides.
Count how many other teams the Opening Government can finish above or below.

acceptedIdeas: All three other teams, including the other Government team
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All three other teams, including the other Government team

choices.label: Only the Opening Opposition, because it replies to them directly
Only the two Opposition teams, because they argue the other side
None of the teams, since the result goes to a whole side
All three other teams, including the other Government team

questions.onCorrect: Being on the same side doesn't make two teams partners, so the Closing Government has to do better than the Opening Government to rank above it.

misconceptions.feedback: The Opposition teams are rivals, but with four rankings to win, the other Government team is a rival as well.
The Opening Opposition is a rival, but so are the Closing Government and the Closing Opposition, since all four teams are ranked against one another.
The judges rank teams, not sides, so a team on the stronger side can still finish last.

questions.prompt: An opponent rises to offer a point of information 6 minutes 30 seconds into a 7-minute speech. What should the speaker do?
hints: Which minutes of a 7-minute speech are protected?
Where does 6 minutes 30 seconds fall in the speech?

acceptedIdeas: Decline it, because the last minute of a speech is protected
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decline it, because the last minute of a speech is protected

choices.label: Decline it, because the last minute of a speech is protected
Accept it, because a speaker should accept at least one point
Accept or decline, since points can be offered at any time

questions.onCorrect: The first and last minute are protected, so points may be offered only between 1 minute and 6 minutes. At 6 minutes 30 seconds the point is out of order.

misconceptions.feedback: That advice applies inside the open window. In the last minute no point may be offered, so there is nothing to accept.
Points cannot be offered at any time. The first and last minute of every speech are protected.

questions.prompt: A round has eight speeches of 7 minutes, and each team has two speakers. How long does one team speak in all?
hints: How many speeches does each team give?
Multiply that by the length of one speech.

acceptedIdeas: 14 minutes, from two speeches
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 14 minutes, from two speeches

choices.label: 7 minutes, from one speech
14 minutes, from two speeches
28 minutes, from four speeches

questions.onCorrect: Two speeches of 7 minutes make 14 minutes, and four teams at 14 minutes each come to the 56 minutes of the round.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 minutes is one speech. Each team has two speakers, and each gives a speech.
28 minutes would be four speeches, which is two teams. One team has two speakers.

questions.prompt: A coach says that points of information can be offered during all 56 minutes of the round. What is wrong with that?
hints: How many minutes of each speech are open to points?
Multiply that by the number of speeches in the round.

acceptedIdeas: Protected minutes at each end leave only 40 of the 56 open
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Protected minutes at each end leave only 40 of the 56 open

choices.label: Points may be offered only in the first and last minute
Nothing is wrong, since the other side may rise at any moment
Protected minutes at each end leave only 40 of the 56 open

questions.onCorrect: Each 7-minute speech has 5 open minutes, and 8 × 5 = 40. The other 16 minutes are protected, which lets each speaker open and close without interruption.

misconceptions.feedback: It is the other way round. The first and last minute are protected, and points are offered between them.
Protected time exists so that every speaker can open and close without interruption.

questions.prompt: A league round uses 5-minute speeches, and the first and last minute are still protected. How does the protected share compare with a 7-minute speech?
hints: Write the protected time as a share of the whole speech in each case.
Divide 2 by 5 and 2 by 7.

acceptedIdeas: It is larger, 40 percent of the speech against about 29 percent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is larger, 40 percent of the speech against about 29 percent

choices.label: It is larger, 40 percent of the speech against about 29 percent
It is the same, because two minutes are protected in both speeches
It is smaller, because a shorter speech has less to protect

questions.onCorrect: Two of five minutes is 40 percent and two of seven is about 29 percent, so a shorter speech loses a larger share to protected time.

misconceptions.feedback: The same two minutes are a larger share of a shorter speech: 40 percent of 5 against about 29 percent of 7.
The protected minutes do not shrink with the speech, so they take a larger share of it.

questions.prompt: The Government Whip's speech introduces a new argument about cost that nobody has raised. How is it likely to be treated?
hints: What are the Whips there to do?
Which speakers are expected to bring extensions?

acceptedIdeas: As out of place, since a Whip summarises and adds nothing new
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As out of place, since a Whip summarises and adds nothing new

choices.label: As an extension, because it is a new line of argument
As a fair summary, because the Whip speaks for the whole side
As out of place, since a Whip summarises and adds nothing new

questions.onCorrect: The two Whips give the last speeches and summarise the debate, so a new argument arrives too late to be weighed against the others.

misconceptions.feedback: An extension belongs to the first speakers of the Closing teams, who build it with a mechanism and an impact. The Whips summarise.
A summary reviews what has been said in the debate. A new cost argument summarises nothing.

questions.prompt: The judges rank the Opening Government first and the Closing Government fourth. What does the result show?
hints: How many rankings are there in a round?
Is the result given to a side or to each team?

acceptedIdeas: Teams on one side are ranked separately and can finish far apart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Teams on one side are ranked separately and can finish far apart

choices.label: Teams on one side are ranked separately and can finish far apart
A mistake, because both teams on one side must share a rank
That the Government side lost, because fourth place decides the side

questions.onCorrect: Each of the four teams is ranked against the other three, and one of those three is on its own side. That is why the Closing Government has to offer something the Opening Government did not.

misconceptions.feedback: Each team is ranked against the other three, so teams on one side can finish far apart.
There is no result for a side. Four teams are ranked from first to fourth.

questions.prompt: The Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition have already spoken. In what order do the other six speakers follow?
hints: The sides alternate, with the Government first.
The Opening teams speak first, then the Closing teams, and the Whips come last.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Deputy Prime Minister and the Deputy Leader of the Opposition come third and fourth, then the Member for the Government and the Member for the Opposition, and the Government Whip and the Opposition Whip close the debate.

questions.onCorrect: The sides alternate throughout, and the order runs Opening team, Closing team, Whips. The Opposition Whip gives the eighth and last speech.

questions.prompt: Impact A would help 1,000 people with probability 0.3, and Impact B would help 200 people with probability 0.9. On average, which helps more people?
hints: Shrink each impact by its chance of happening.
A keeps about a third of its 1,000, while B keeps nearly all of its 200.

acceptedIdeas: A helps more, but not nearly five times as many
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A helps more, but not nearly five times as many

choices.label: They help about the same number of people
B helps more, because it is almost certain to happen
A helps more, but not nearly five times as many
A helps about five times as many people as B

questions.onCorrect: Scaled by their chances, A comes to about 300 and B to about 180, so A is ahead by far less than its headline size suggests.

misconceptions.feedback: Near-certainty counts for a lot, but 0.3 of 1,000 is still more than 0.9 of 200.
A works out at about 300 people on average and B at about 180, which is a clear gap.
A's size is cut to about a third by its probability, while B's is barely cut, so the five-to-one gap shrinks a great deal.

questions.prompt: Impact B would help 200 people with probability 0.9. How should a team describe its size?
hints: Multiply the number affected by the probability.
A chance of 0.9 means that one time in ten nobody is helped.

acceptedIdeas: About 180 people on average, since it might not happen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 180 people on average, since it might not happen

choices.label: About 222 people, once the chance of 0.9 is divided out
About 180 people on average, since it might not happen
200 people, since the chance of success is high

questions.onCorrect: 200 × 0.9 = 180. Expected size puts the number affected and the chance on one scale.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing by the probability gives a larger number, which is the wrong direction. Expected size is the number multiplied by the probability.
A high chance is still not a certain one. Multiplying by 0.9 gives the average.

questions.prompt: Impact A has an expected size of 300 and Impact B an expected size of 180. A team says: "A is bigger, so A wins." What should a weighing sentence add?
hints: The gap between 300 and 180 is on one axis only. Which other axes can impacts be weighed on?
A good weighing concedes what is true on the other side.

acceptedIdeas: Timeframe and reversibility, since size is only one axis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Timeframe and reversibility, since size is only one axis

choices.label: Timeframe and reversibility, since size is only one axis
Nothing, because the larger expected size decides the round
That B counts for nothing, since A is larger

questions.onCorrect: A is larger by 120, which is a statement about magnitude and probability. Weighing goes on to name the other axes and say why they favour a side.

misconceptions.feedback: Size is one axis. A smaller impact can win on timeframe or reversibility, and a judge needs the team to say why its axis matters most.
Treating the other side's impact as zero is rarely believable. A good weighing concedes what is true and then compares.

questions.prompt: A team has written a 900-word case for a 4-minute slot and speaks at about 150 words a minute. What follows?
hints: How many words does a 4-minute slot hold at 150 words a minute?
Compare the draft with that budget before you think about speaking faster.

acceptedIdeas: It runs about 6 minutes, so it needs cutting by around 300 words
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It runs about 6 minutes, so it needs cutting by around 300 words

choices.label: It fits, because 900 words is under 1,050, the size of a full speech
It runs about 6 minutes, so it needs cutting by around 300 words
It fits if the team speaks at about 225 words a minute

questions.onCorrect: A 4-minute slot holds about 600 words, and 900 words at 150 a minute runs about 6 minutes, so around 300 words have to go.

misconceptions.feedback: 1,050 words is the budget for a 7-minute speech and not a 4-minute one. A 4-minute case holds about 600 words.
225 a minute is far above the 120 to 160 guide and flattens emphasis. The case should be cut and the pace left alone.

questions.prompt: Free buses might lead 40,000 commuters to switch from driving, but only with probability 0.25. Which description of the impact is fair?
hints: Multiply the number who might switch by the probability that they do.
A probability of 0.25 is one chance in four.

acceptedIdeas: On average 10,000 commuters switch
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On average 10,000 commuters switch

choices.label: On average 160,000 commuters switch
40,000 commuters switch
On average 10,000 commuters switch

questions.onCorrect: 40,000 × 0.25 = 10,000. The impact is comparable with other impacts once it is put on this scale.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing 40,000 by 0.25 gives 160,000, which is the wrong direction. Multiply by the probability.
That states the best outcome as if it were certain. A probability of 0.25 cuts it to a quarter.

questions.prompt: Free buses might lead to service cuts that hurt 12,000 riders, with probability 0.3. Set beside the Government's 10,000, what is the Opposition's expected size?
hints: Multiply the number hurt by the probability.
Put the result beside 10,000 on the same scale.

acceptedIdeas: About 3,600 riders, well below the Government's 10,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 3,600 riders, well below the Government's 10,000

choices.label: About 3,600 riders, well below the Government's 10,000
12,000 riders, which is larger than the Government's 10,000
About 400 riders, since 12,000 divided by 30 is 400

questions.onCorrect: 12,000 × 0.3 = 3,600, which is well below the Government's 10,000. The Opposition would then have to argue on other axes.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full harm and ignores its probability. At 0.3 the expected harm is 3,600.
0.3 is thirty percent and not one in thirty. Thirty percent of 12,000 is 3,600.

questions.prompt: An invented team argues for free school meals. Sort its five statements into claim, mechanism and impact.
hints: A mechanism explains how the claim would come about, and an impact says why it matters.
Ask "how?" or "so what?" of each statement.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every child being offered a meal is the claim. Hungry children concentrating and the end of stigma are mechanisms, and more qualifications and lower food bills are impacts.

items.label: Every child should be offered a free school meal
items.explanation: It is the statement the team wants the judges to accept.

items.label: Hungry children cannot concentrate, so a meal raises the attention they give to lessons
items.explanation: It explains how the claim would come about.

items.label: A shared meal for everyone removes the stigma of being singled out
items.explanation: It explains a second way the claim would come about.

items.label: More children finish school with qualifications
items.explanation: It says why the claim matters.

items.label: Families on tight budgets spend less on food
items.explanation: It says why the claim matters to a second group.

questions.onCorrect: A case is a claim with a mechanism that makes it happen and an impact that makes it matter.

questions.prompt: Impact X helps 50,000 people with probability 0.002. Impact Y helps 80 people with probability 0.9. How much larger is X's expected size than Y's?
hints: Work out each expected size first.
X is 100 and Y is 72, so subtract.
questions.onCorrect: X wins narrowly on expected size, although it is the far less likely impact, so timeframe and reversibility could still decide the round.

misconceptions.feedback: That is X's expected size alone. Subtract Y's expected size, 72.
That is Y's expected size. Subtract it from X's, 100.

questions.prompt: The Closing Opposition's first speaker rebuts the Government's case again in fresh words, and a judge says the speech added no extension. Why?
hints: An extension has to give the judges a reason to rank the team above its own opening team.
Does saying the same rebuttal in new words add a new line of argument?

acceptedIdeas: An extension is a new line of argument, and a fresh rebuttal is not one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An extension is a new line of argument, and a fresh rebuttal is not one

choices.label: An extension must come from the Whips, who speak last
Fresh words count as an extension only if the examples are new
An extension is a new line of argument, and a fresh rebuttal is not one

questions.onCorrect: A new rebuttal of the same case adds nothing the Opening Opposition did not already offer. An extension is new and separate, and it is built with a mechanism and an impact.

misconceptions.feedback: Extensions come from the first speakers of the Closing teams. The Whips summarise.
New examples for the same arguments are a repeat. An extension is a new and separate line of argument.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "The bridge will surely open on time, because the work is on schedule." A listener points out that a strike is planned for the week before the opening. Which reply keeps the claim in line with its support?
hints: Look at the word *surely*. Does a schedule justify that much strength?
A planned strike is a condition under which the warrant could fail. How would a careful speaker allow for it in the claim?

acceptedIdeas: The bridge will probably open on time, unless the strike goes ahead
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The bridge will probably open on time, unless the strike goes ahead

choices.label: The bridge will surely open on time, as I said at the start
The bridge will open on time, so the strike does not matter here
The bridge will never open on time now that a strike is planned
The bridge will probably open on time, unless the strike goes ahead

questions.onCorrect: *Probably* sets the strength of the claim and *unless* names the condition that would break it. The speaker now has to say whether the strike will happen, which a listener can check.

misconceptions.feedback: Saying it again with the same strength is confidence, and confidence is not evidence. The strike is a condition that could break the schedule.
That waves the exception away without saying why it does not apply. A fair reply says whether the condition holds in this case.
That overcorrects. A planned strike is a reason to soften the claim, and it is not support for the opposite one.

questions.prompt: A councillor says: "We cut the limit on Station Road to 20 mph, and accidents there fell from 50 a year to 35, so the cut works." Which closed question tests the exception that accidents were already falling?
hints: The exception is that accidents were already falling.
A good closed question is short, neutral and can be answered yes or no.

acceptedIdeas: Had accidents already been falling before the cut?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Had accidents already been falling before the cut?

questions.onCorrect: The question is neutral and names the exception, so a yes concedes it and a no gives you a firm statement to hold the councillor to.

choices.label: Why did you choose 20 mph and not 30?
Surely the accidents were falling anyway, weren't they?
Do you not think the cut was a waste of money?
Had accidents already been falling before the cut?

misconceptions.feedback: That is an open question, and it does not test whether the fall had another cause. A closed question names the exception and can be answered yes or no.
That is a closed question, but it is leading: it tells the councillor the answer you expect. A fair closed question is neutral.
That is loaded, and it moves to cost, which is not the exception. The question should test whether the fall had another cause.

questions.prompt: A proposes a 20 mph limit near the school, and B replies: "So you want everyone to crawl everywhere at 20?" Which reply from A describes the difference calmly and hands the conversation back?
hints: A good reply says what B changed and then returns to the proposal.
Which reply puts A's actual words back in front of the room?

acceptedIdeas: I said near the school, not everywhere. Can we talk about that stretch of road?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: I said near the school, not everywhere. Can we talk about that stretch of road?

questions.onCorrect: The reply says calmly what A actually proposed and hands the room a question about that proposal.

choices.label: That's a straw man, and I won't answer it until you apologise for twisting my words.
I said near the school, not everywhere. Can we talk about that stretch of road?
You always twist what people say, and everyone in this room has noticed it by now.
Yes, if that is what it takes, everyone should crawl everywhere at 20 miles an hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That names the move but offers the room nothing to check, and it asks for an apology in place of an answer to the proposal.
That is an attack on B, and it hands the room a quarrel in place of a question about the road.
That accepts B's distorted version as if it were the proposal. A's actual proposal was a limit near the school.

questions.prompt: A councillor wants to answer a proposal to plant trees along Mill Road, and means to follow Rapoport's rules. In what order do the parts of the reply go?
hints: Rapoport's rules put the other person's view before your own.
Criticism is allowed, but only after three other things have been done.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Restate the proposal first, then list the points of agreement, then say what you learned, and only then give your criticism.

items: Restate the proposal so fairly that its supporters would accept it
Say what you have learned from them

questions.onCorrect: The first three steps are all about the other person's view, so by the time the criticism comes the speaker has heard that you understood. A rebuttal that comes first is heard as a dodge.

questions.prompt: The other side says a safer road design costs more, and they are right. Which sentence makes a concession and weighs it?
hints: A concession grants the point first and then weighs it.
Which sentence still argues for your side after granting the cost?

acceptedIdeas: It costs more, and I grant that, but it saves lives, and I'd argue lives outweigh cost.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It costs more, and I grant that, but it saves lives, and I'd argue lives outweigh cost.

questions.onCorrect: A concession lets you argue from strength, since you have admitted the cost and still explained why your side should win.

choices.label: It costs more, but I'd argue that cost should never be a factor in how we build a road.
It costs more, and so I withdraw the proposal, since the other side is plainly right.
It costs more, and I grant that, but it saves lives, and I'd argue lives outweigh cost.
It saves lives, and the other side has said nothing about that, so there is nothing to grant.

misconceptions.feedback: That mentions the cost in a clause and then dismisses it. A concession weighs the cost against what your side offers.
That concedes the point and gives up the whole argument. A concession grants one point and then argues that your side outweighs it.
That refuses to grant a point the other side has fairly made, which is the opposite of a concession.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks: "Has the contractor been paid yet?" It has not. Which answer is the best start?
hints: It asks about a plain fact, and it has two possible answers.
A direct question deserves a direct answer.

acceptedIdeas: No, not yet. What matters is that payment follows the final inspection.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, not yet. What matters is that payment follows the final inspection.

questions.onCorrect: A direct question about a fact needs the plain answer before any bridge, because a listener will not hear the bridge until the question has been answered.

choices.label: That is a good question, and one I have been asked several times this week.
What matters is that the work is finished to a high standard, and it will be.
No, not yet. What matters is that payment follows the final inspection.
Payment is a complicated matter, and it depends on a number of different things.

misconceptions.feedback: That stalls, and the listener is still waiting for a yes or a no.
A bridge that comes before the plain answer sounds like evasion, even when it is true. A direct question deserves its answer first.
That is vague. The question has a plain answer, and a plain answer comes first.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks what the repair will cost, and the final quote has not arrived. Which answer keeps your credibility?
hints: An honest answer says what you do not know and what happens next.
Which options claim knowledge you do not have?

acceptedIdeas: I don't have a figure yet. The quote arrives on Friday, and I'll share it then.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: I don't have a figure yet. The quote arrives on Friday, and I'll share it then.

questions.onCorrect: Saying that you do not have the figure, and when you will, is honest, and a speaker who does this is believed when they do have it.

choices.label: I don't have a figure yet. The quote arrives on Friday, and I'll share it then.
It will cost nothing at all, because the budget already covers the whole repair.
No comment on costs until the work is finished and every bill has been paid.
It will be less than people expect, so there is no need for anyone to worry.

misconceptions.feedback: That claims knowledge you do not have, and a later figure would damage your credibility.
Listeners hear no comment as concealment, and it gives them nothing.
That sounds like an answer but gives no figure, and listeners notice the evasion.

questions.prompt: You are pitching a four-week trial of a new rota to a shop owner. Which call to action is best?
hints: A good call to action names a step and a time.
Which option tells the owner exactly what to do?

acceptedIdeas: Agree to a four-week trial of the new rota, starting on 1 March.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Agree to a four-week trial of the new rota, starting on 1 March.

questions.onCorrect: It names the step, agreeing to the trial, and the time, starting on 1 March, so the owner knows exactly what to do next.

choices.label: Think about whether a new rota could suit the shop in the future.
Agree to a four-week trial of the new rota, starting on 1 March.
Let's all work together towards a fairer and happier shop for everyone.
Give the new rota your support, if you feel that you are able to.

misconceptions.feedback: That names no step and no time, so the owner can agree without doing anything.
That names no step and no time. It is a wish and not an ask.
That asks for sympathy and not for a step, so the owner would not know what to do.

questions.prompt: A salesperson presses a free sample into your hand and then says it would be rude not to buy something. Which of Cialdini's six principles is being abused?
hints: The sample is a favour, and the pressure comes from owing one.
One principle is the urge to return a favour.

acceptedIdeas: reciprocity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: reciprocity

questions.onCorrect: Reciprocity is honest when a favour is freely given, and manipulation when it is used to create a debt that the listener feels they must repay.

misconceptions.feedback: Scarcity concerns limited supply. The salesperson is using a favour to make you feel you owe something.
Authority concerns trusted experts. The salesperson is using a favour to make you feel you owe something.
Liking concerns affinity with the speaker. The salesperson is using a favour to make you feel you owe something.
Social proof concerns doing what others do. The salesperson is using a favour to make you feel you owe something.

questions.prompt: Which of these fails the transparency test?
hints: Ask whether you would be comfortable with the listener seeing how and why you used the technique.
Which option depends on the listener not knowing something?

acceptedIdeas: Saying the offer ends today when you can extend it any time.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Saying the offer ends today when you can extend it any time.

questions.onCorrect: A deadline that you can move works only if the listener does not know it can move, so it would not survive being seen.

choices.label: Telling a donor a true story about a family the charity helped.
Saying the offer ends today when you can extend it any time.
Showing an audience your own sales figures, poor months included.
Quoting a heart specialist on the side effects of a heart drug.

misconceptions.feedback: A true story about a real family can be shown openly, so it passes the test.
Showing your own figures, poor months included, can be done openly, so it passes the test.
Quoting a relevant expert can be shown openly, so it passes the test.

questions.prompt: You are the Member for the Opposition, the first speaker of the Closing Opposition. What is your main job?
hints: Closing teams are ranked against their own opening team too. What would earn a higher rank?
The Whips summarise and the opening speakers define. What is left for the first closing speaker?

acceptedIdeas: Add a new line of argument that the opening team missed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a new line of argument that the opening team missed

choices.label: Summarise the whole debate and add no new arguments
Add a new line of argument that the opening team missed
Define the motion and then present the opposition case

questions.onCorrect: The Member's speech must offer an extension, a new line of argument that gives the judges a reason to rank the team above its own opening team.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the job of the Whips in the last two speeches. A Member comes earlier and has to bring something new.
The opening speakers define the motion. A closing speaker works inside that definition.

questions.prompt: The Closing Government's first speaker makes the same two arguments as the Prime Minister, with fresh examples. How are the judges likely to see the speech?
hints: The closing team is a rival of its own side's opening team.
Ask whether the judges have been given anything new.

acceptedIdeas: As a repeat of the opening case, with no reason to rank the team higher
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a repeat of the opening case, with no reason to rank the team higher

questions.onCorrect: A repeat gives the judges nothing new to rank, so the closing team has to bring an extension, a new and separate line of argument.

choices.label: As an extension, because the examples are new even if the arguments are not
As a repeat of the opening case, with no reason to rank the team higher
As a fair summary, because closing teams are there to sum up the debate

misconceptions.feedback: An extension is a new line of argument. New examples for the same two arguments leave the opening team's case where it was.
Summarising is the Whips' job, in the last two speeches. A closing team's first speaker must bring a new line of argument.

questions.prompt: For the motion "This House would ban advertising aimed at children", which side carries the burden of showing that the change would be better?
hints: The side proposing the change carries the burden.
In this format it is the side that argues for the motion.

acceptedIdeas: The Government
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Government

questions.onCorrect: The Government proposes the change, so it must show that the change would be better, and the Opposition may show that it would not.

choices.label: The Government
The Opposition

misconceptions.feedback: The Opposition argues against the motion. The side that proposes the change carries the burden of showing it would be better.

questions.prompt: A speaker says "Smaller classes help pupils" and explains that a smaller class gives each pupil more of the teacher's time, but never says why that matters. What is missing?
hints: Ask "how?" of the claim and "so what?" of the mechanism.
The speaker has answered one of those questions. Which one is left?

acceptedIdeas: An impact, the answer to "so what?"
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An impact, the answer to "so what?"

choices.label: A mechanism, since the speaker has not said how classes help
A weighing against the other side's case
An impact, the answer to "so what?"

questions.onCorrect: The mechanism says how the claim would come about and the impact says why it matters. Without an impact the judge has nothing to weigh.

misconceptions.feedback: The speaker has given one: more of the teacher's time for each pupil. What is missing comes after it.
Weighing comes once both sides have impacts. This argument has not got one yet.

questions.prompt: A team's impact is smaller than the other side's, but it arrives next year and is almost certain. Which weighing sentence is best?
hints: A good weighing sentence concedes what is true and compares on named axes.
Which option names probability and timeframe?

acceptedIdeas: Theirs is larger, but ours is likelier and comes next year.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Theirs is larger, but ours is likelier and comes next year.

questions.onCorrect: It concedes the other side's size, and then names the axes, probability and timeframe, on which the team's impact is stronger.

choices.label: Ours is smaller, but a small impact is still better than none.
Theirs is larger, but ours is likelier and comes next year.
Theirs will not happen, so it should count for nothing here.
Ours matters more, because it feels more real to the people involved.

misconceptions.feedback: That concedes the size but names no axis, so the judge has nothing to weigh.
That treats the other side's impact as nothing, which is rarely believable and easy to rebut.
Emotion is not an axis of comparison. The judge needs size, probability, timeframe or reversibility.

flashcards.front: What word names the statement a speaker wants you to accept?
flashcards.back: The claim is the statement the whole speech is built to make you accept.

acceptedIdeas: claim
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: claim

flashcards.front: The word because appears in both explanations and arguments. How can you tell which one a speaker is giving?
flashcards.back: Ask whether the listener already accepts the fact being given a cause: if so it is an explanation, and if not the speaker is arguing.

flashcards.front: A listener says "You're wrong" to a speaker. Why does that give the speaker little to answer, and what should the listener name instead?
flashcards.back: It names no part of the argument, so the speaker can only repeat the claim, whereas a challenge to the grounds or the warrant points at something specific.

flashcards.front: What is Toulmin's name for words like "presumably" and "probably" that set how strongly a claim is made?
flashcards.back: A qualifier says how strong the claim is, and a bold claim with weak support is the easiest to push on.

acceptedIdeas: qualifier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: qualifier

flashcards.front: What do we call a reply that answers the speaker as a person instead of answering the argument?
flashcards.back: An ad hominem answers the person, which leaves the argument itself untouched.

acceptedIdeas: ad hominem
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ad hominem

flashcards.front: You have spotted a fallacy in someone's argument. Why does that not show that their conclusion is false?
flashcards.back: It shows that one reason for the conclusion fails, and the conclusion may still be true on other grounds.

flashcards.front: A risk rises from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. What is the relative change, in percent?
flashcards.back: The rise is 1 in 1,000, which is 1 ÷ 2 = 50 percent of the starting risk.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 1 in 1,000, which is 1 ÷ 2 = 50 percent of the starting risk.

flashcards.front: Which question catches most misleading statistics, and what does it ask for?
flashcards.back: Compared with what asks for the starting figure, the group or the base rate that makes the number meaningful.

flashcards.front: Write the strongest five-sentence version of a view you reject. Would someone who holds it say you had put it fairly?
flashcards.back: A fair restatement shows you understood and makes your reply harder to dismiss.

flashcards.front: What do we call the strongest fair version of the other side's case?
flashcards.back: A steelman is the strongest version of a view, stated so that its holder would accept it.

acceptedIdeas: steelman
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: steelman

flashcards.front: What do the four letters of PREP stand for, in order?
flashcards.back: Point, Reason, Example, Point: the answer first, why, a case, and the answer again.

flashcards.front: About how many words does a speaker say in one minute, as a planning figure?
flashcards.back: About 150 words a minute is a common planning figure, and speakers vary around it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About 150 words a minute is a common planning figure, and speakers vary around it.

flashcards.front: Record a 60-second talk, count your words and fillers, and replace your most common filler with a pause. Rate the second recording against the first.
flashcards.back: Counting before and after shows whether a change worked, which feelings alone can't.

flashcards.front: One speaker has 12 fillers in 4 minutes and another has 5 fillers in 1 minute. Which speaker uses more fillers for the time they speak, and how do you know?
flashcards.back: The second speaker does, at 5 a minute against 3. Counts from talks of different lengths mean little until each is divided by its time.

flashcards.front: Record yourself answering six tough questions about your own view, 30 seconds each. Rate whether each answer dealt with the question before it bridged.
flashcards.back: A bridge only works once the question has had a real answer, and the recording is how you check.

flashcards.front: In ABC, what do you call the short phrase that moves from your answer to your message?
flashcards.back: The bridge is a short phrase, used once, that follows a real answer.

acceptedIdeas: bridge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: bridge

flashcards.front: Record a 2-minute pitch for a view of yours that ends in one specific call to action. Would the audience know exactly what to do next?
flashcards.back: A call to action names a step and a time, and a recording lets you hear whether yours does.

flashcards.front: What three things does an audience analysis ask about the listeners, before it asks what they will do?
flashcards.back: It asks what they know, what they want and what they fear.

flashcards.front: A leaflet says a surgery has a 90 percent survival rate. What would you add so that the listener sees the whole picture, and why?
flashcards.back: Give the other frame too, that 10 in every 100 do not survive. The two descriptions are one fact, and giving both lets the listener see it.

flashcards.front: Why does a technique being effective not make it ethical?
flashcards.back: The test is honesty and respect for the listener's judgement, and manipulation often works because it hides what it is doing.

flashcards.front: In a 7-minute British Parliamentary speech, in which minutes may points of information be offered?
flashcards.back: Points of information are allowed only between the protected first and last minutes, so minutes 2 to 6.

flashcards.front: How many teams take part in a British Parliamentary debate, and how many speakers are in each?
flashcards.back: Four teams of two: Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government and Closing Opposition.

flashcards.front: Record a 4-minute case for a motion and score it from 1 to 5 on role, matter, manner and time. Where did you score lowest?
flashcards.back: A score on each criterion shows what to change in the next recording.

flashcards.front: What four axes can you weigh two impacts on?
flashcards.back: Magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility.

essays.title: A councillor's speech sorted and signposted
essays.prompt:
Sort the speech below into its claim, its reasons and the evidence for each, and pick out the one sentence that explains a fact instead of arguing for the claim. Then rewrite the speech so that a listener could follow it at first hearing. Your version will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

A councillor gave this speech at the public meeting, in this order.

Last summer we closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays. Footfall went from 4,000 to 5,000. Thirty-six of the sixty shops took more money and nine took less. There was one injury on those Saturdays, where there had been four on the twelve before. The street was quiet in August because half the town was away. So we should close Market Street to cars every Saturday. Shops do better, and people are safer.
essays.expectedScope: A short sorted list, one sentence on the explanation, and a speech of 70 to 110 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: States the claim in one sentence, and it is the statement the rest of the speech supports.
Gives two reasons and puts the right evidence under each.
Picks out the sentence that explains an accepted fact and says why it does no work for the claim.
The rewritten speech puts the claim first, marks each reason with a spoken signpost and returns to the claim at the end.
The rewrite keeps the councillor's figures unchanged.

essays.title: Three questions for the weak link
essays.prompt:
Find the weak link in the argument below. State the warrant it leaves unsaid, write three closed questions you would put to the speaker, and then rewrite the claim with a qualifier that the evidence can carry. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write the questions exactly as you would ask them.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

The argument, from a councillor: "Footfall on Market Street rose from 4,000 to 5,000 on the trial Saturdays, so closing the street every Saturday will bring a thousand more customers all year."

The trial ran from the middle of June to the end of August. The summer fair was held on the street on two of the twelve Saturdays, and the footfall counter does not tell a customer from someone walking through.
essays.expectedScope: A warrant, three questions and a rewritten claim: 80 to 140 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: States the warrant as a general rule that the argument needs and never says.
One question tests whether the facts are true and complete, one tests whether they support the claim, and one raises a condition under which the rule fails.
Each question can be answered with yes, no or a number.
The rewritten claim carries a qualifier, and the qualifier matches a limit of the trial.

essays.title: Replies to four remarks from the floor
essays.prompt:
Write a reply to each of the four remarks below, as you would give it from the chair of the meeting. Each reply has two parts, the first saying in plain words what the remark did and the second taking the meeting back to the question. Your replies will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday. The chair of the traders' association, who owns a furniture shop, has spoken against the closure. A councillor has spoken for it.

(1) "Of course she is against it. She sells sofas."

(2) "The councillor wants to ban cars from Alderby."

(3) "Either we close the street or we watch the town centre die."

(4) "My neighbour's shop took less on those Saturdays, so the trial was bad for the shops."
essays.expectedScope: Four replies of two sentences each: 100 to 170 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: Each reply says in plain words what the remark did, and the description fits that remark.
No reply relies on a label alone, such as a Latin name, to make its point.
Each reply ends by returning the meeting to a question about the closure that can be checked.
At least one reply grants that the speaker's conclusion might still be right for other reasons.
Each reply is short enough to say in one breath.

essays.title: The trial's numbers said fairly
essays.prompt:
Write the part of a speech that reports the trial's results to the public meeting, fairly enough that neither side could call it slanted. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

These are the trial's figures. Saturday footfall on the street rose from 4,000 people to 5,000. Of the street's 60 shops, 36 took more money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 9 took less, and those 9 mostly sell furniture, appliances and garden supplies. There was 1 injury on the street during the twelve trial Saturdays and there had been 4 on the twelve Saturdays before. Traffic on Mill Lane, the next street, rose from 300 vehicles an hour to 420. Eight parking bays for blue badge holders were out of use, and the nearest others are 250 metres away. Barriers and two stewards cost £900 each Saturday.
essays.expectedScope: A passage of 110 to 170 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Gives the rise in footfall as a number of people and as a percentage of the starting figure, and both are right.
Gives the shops that gained and the shops that lost as shares of the 60.
Reports the injuries without claiming more than counts of four and one can show, and says why.
Gives the change on Mill Lane, so that the cost to the next street is in the account.
Names one comparison that the trial did not make and a careful listener would ask for.

essays.title: A steelman and a rebuttal of the traders' case
essays.prompt:
You are speaking for the closure, straight after the speech below. Restate the traders' case so fairly that its speaker would accept your version, say where you agree, and then rebut it with one move. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

The chair of the traders' association said this: "Nine shops took less money, and they are the ones that sell what you cannot carry home on foot. Eight blue badge bays went out of use, and the nearest are 250 metres away. Mill Lane took 420 vehicles an hour where it had taken 300. The barriers and stewards cost £900 every Saturday. Leave the street open."

You also know that 36 of the street's 60 shops took more money on the trial Saturdays and that footfall rose from 4,000 to 5,000.
essays.expectedScope: A reply of 120 to 190 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Restates the traders' case with its strongest point included, in words its speaker would accept.
Names a point of agreement before any criticism.
Makes one rebuttal, and a reader can tell whether it denies the evidence, denies the link, gives an exception, or concedes and outweighs.
Concedes something specific, with its figure.
Gives reasons for your own claim and does not ask the traders to disprove it.

essays.title: A one-minute answer, written out
essays.prompt:
The chair of the meeting turns to you and asks: "Should Market Street be closed to cars every Saturday?" Write the answer you would give in one minute, in favour or against, using the PREP pattern. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Gives a reason and then an example that uses a figure from the trial.
Is between 135 and 165 words long.
Marks its parts with spoken signposts and holds no more than three points.
Is written for the ear: no sentence is too long to say in one breath, and no figure appears that a listener could not repeat.

essays.title: A rehearsal note on pace and nerves
essays.prompt:
Write yourself a note after the rehearsal described below. Work out your pace and your filler rate, say how many words the script has to lose, choose one target for the next run, and say how you will handle the nerves. The note is written work and will be read here, not heard.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday. You have a slot of two minutes at the public meeting.

You rehearsed once with a timer and a friend. Your script has 390 words and you got through all of it in exactly 2 minutes. Your friend counted 14 fillers such as "um" and "you know", and said that the three figures in the middle went past too fast to catch. You plan at 150 words a minute. Your heart was racing before you began.
essays.expectedScope: A note of 90 to 150 words. Allow about 8 minutes.
successCriteria: Gives the pace and the filler rate of the rehearsal, both worked correctly from the figures.
Says how many words the script must lose to fit two minutes at the planning pace.
Chooses one target for the next rehearsal and says how it will be measured.
Says where a pause would help and what job the pause does there.
Handles the nerves in the way the lesson's research supports, and does not claim more for it than the research does.

essays.title: Answers to three hard questions
essays.prompt:
You have spoken for closing Market Street every Saturday, and the questions begin. Write your key message, and then your answer to each of the three questions below. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday. Of the street's 60 shops, 36 took more money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 9 took less. The trial ran only in summer, and nobody has measured Mill Lane, the next street, in winter.

(1) "Did any shop take less money during the trial?"

(2) "Why are you so determined to kill off the furniture shops?"

(3) "What will this do to the traffic on Mill Lane in December?"
essays.expectedScope: A key message and three answers of two or three sentences each: 100 to 170 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: The key message is 20 words or fewer and says what you want the listener to keep.
The first answer gives its yes or no, with the figure, before anything else.
The second answer does not repeat the question's loaded words in your own voice.
The third answer says what you do not know and what you will do about it.
Each answer reaches the key message by a bridge that follows from what was asked.

essays.title: One opening for two rooms

You will make the case for closing Market Street to two audiences in one week: the traders' association on Tuesday and the town's disability access forum on Thursday. Write a line of audience analysis for each, and then the opening of each talk. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.
